speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: EUROPEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity to report to the House on my trip last week to western Europe. In doing so, I am very pleased to be able to say that in both Paris and Brussels I found evidence of considerable warmth towards Canada, considerable interest in Canadian attitudes, and considerable desire to seek a convergence of interests. I can assure this House, Mr. Speaker, that in those places and within the international organizations sited there, the reputation of Canada is high. I can assure the House equally that there exists within the governments of France, Belgium and Luxembourg a genuine and wholesome appreciation of the Canadian fact.
It goes without saying that the discussions in Paris with President Giscard d'Estaing and with Prime Minister Chirac and other ministers took place against a background of deep historical bonds and a shared culture of considerable richness. Of equal importance, however, they took place in an environment which acknowledged the distinctiveness of the Canadian entity and the modernity of Canadian accomplishments. There was evident in those meetings, a will to deal practically with issues; a desire to cooperate rather than compete, to participate rather than withdraw, to consult rather than assume.
We agreed while in Paris to launch two bilateral working groups each with an objective of identifying areas of fruitful cooperation in order to increase and diversify our volume of trade. Each is to conclude its work in time to report to the Canada-France Joint Economic Committee at its next meeting to be held in Ottawa in the first half of next year. One working group will concentrate on examining, without advance commitment, technological and trade investment possibilities with respect to petroleum, gas, coal and nuclear fuels, taking into account matters of interest to both sides. The other group will examine the rather broader area of trade potential in industrial sectors and in the first instance would concentrate on the transportation industry, dealing with French interests in railways and in helicopters and with Canadian interests in STOL aircraft and in all-terrain vehicles.
An indication of the importance attached to these decisions was the agreement that the next Joint Economic
Committee meeting take place-for the first time-at the ministerial level.
Finally, it was recognized that the ultimate success of the work to be undertaken rested largely with private enterprise and that special efforts should be made to bring together French and Canadian businessmen in the coming months. In this connection, I have asked the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) to lead an official trade mission of Canadian businessmen to France in 1975.
In Brussels, where I profited from formal discussions with Prime Minister Tindemans and his cabinet colleagues, as well as with Prime Minister Thorn of Luxembourg, the same intensity of purpose was manifest: to build on the warm relations now existing with Canada, to intensify the contacts and exchanges now pursued, to support Canadian initiatives with the European community, to co-operate in multilateral sectors.
In Brussels too, as in Paris earlier in the week, there was broad agreement not simply on the identification of the major issues of global proportions but also on the postures which must be adopted with respect to them. We discussed, and agreed, that the dangers of nuclear proliferation demanded the design and implementation of more thorough and effective safeguards. We also agreed that the critical elements of the present state of the world economy-inflation, slow growth, balance of payments deficits, recycling, trade negotiations-demanded liberal and statesmanlike attitudes as distinct from cautious and protectionist ones. In this latter respect, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and I have now sought and received the views and understanding of no less than eight prime ministers and presidents in the last six weeks. We shall continue our efforts in weeks to come.
Western Europe is, of course, much more than the geographical location of several nation states. It is, as well, the site of a number of international organizations: in Paris, UNESCO and OECD; in Brussels, NATO, and others elsewhere. It is still something else; it is an evolving concept, a process, an idea to which dedicated men, in spite of formidable obstacles, are bending their efforts through the growing and ever maturing European community. This Europe is not the sum of the national parts; it exists of them and for them, yet it exists in addition to them. It is not enough, Jean Monnet was fond of saying, to add together the several sovereignties; men had to create the new Europe. They are now engaged slowly, sometimes painfully, in that creative process. This Europe, this entity of the future, is organic in nature. As yet, its potential size and strength and attitudes can only be conjectured. But

October 28, 1974
European Economic Community
one fails at one's peril to recognize the sense of destiny which fuels this evolution.
Our government recognizes that emerging fact, Mr. Speaker, and we applaud it. We applauded last week in Brussels, just as we applauded two years ago on the occasion of the entry into the community of Britain, Ireland and Denmark. And these expressions of understanding have coloured the way in which our current approach to the European community has been received. That initiative, Mr. Speaker, is no less and no more than to seek ways of engaging the community in a dynamic, co-operative enterprise.
We wish to add a new, yet parallel dimension to the expanding links we are already building with our partners among the nine member states; a relationship which will grow as the community itself moves from infancy through adolescence to full maturity; a relationship in which Canada's interests and its singular identity are recognized and reflected in decisions taken; a relationship in which consultation and reciprocal advice are accepted; a relationship, Mr. Speaker, of mutual respect, of give and take.
There is a degree of novelty to this exercise. The community, understandably, is as yet far from certain of the shape it will assume, the jurisdiction it will occupy, or the powers it will possess in years to come. Nor is it for Canada to say. This is a European exercise. Yet one thing is certain. It is that this new Europe-which already accounts for 20 per cent of world trade-will be an increasingly formidable actor on the world stage: in commerce, in science, in economic and financial activity, in technology and more. That being the case, it would be irresponsible for a Canadian government not to seek a distinctive relationship with it. Without question, such an exercise could be conducted along more familiar channels were we to wait a few years, as most other countries have apparently chosen to do. But that would ignore the advantages to be gained from engaging the community at an early stage; that would ignore the spirit of creativity which now permeates the community and to which we seek to contribute. Comfort and familiarity are not our criteria; benefit to Canada is.
This desire, this technique, this goal, is shared by the European commission, Mr. Speaker. Our discussions with President Ortoli, with Vice-President Soames and with other commissioners, left no doubt about this. There was a significant meeting of minds both on the concept of this new relationship and on the initial steps to set the process in motion. It is bound to be a lengthy process, but we must begin. As a result of my talks in Brussels, it was agreed that a new process would be initiated involving concrete steps to strengthen the links between Canada and the European community. The parties agreed to begin exploratory talks in the near future on the nature and scope of negotiations intended to define the form and content of the relationship between them.
For this purpose, Canadian and community officials have been instructed to schedule meetings without delay. In addition, the president of the commission has agreed to visit Ottawa at an early date. I am also pleased that a full delegation office will be opened in Ottawa in 1975, of the same nature as those already operating in Washington and Tokyo.


I invite all hon. members to share in this process. Happily, an increased opportunity to do so will soon exist as a result of a further agreement reached last week. While in Paris, I was able to announce, with the approval of the French Government, that the Canadian Government would open a Consulate General in Strasbourg. This office will permit a Canadian presence to be extended into an important region of France for the benefit of our commercial, cultural, information and immigration programs and for the extension of services to Canadian tourists and businessmen. It will also support an enhancement of present links between the Parliament of Canada and the Parliament of Europe, and with the Council of Europe. As Honourable Members are aware, the European Parliament is situated in Strasbourg, and is expected to perform an increasingly important role in the new European Community. I place great importance on such links and on the constructive contribution offered by Canadian parliamentarians. Again and again in Europe I was told of the respect and the high reputation which delegations from this Parliament have earned through their hard work when abroad. It was my good fortune to be in Paris while one such delegation was present and to note the great distinction with which it did its work.
I have already mentioned, Mr. Speaker, the presence in Paris and Brussels of several international bodies of considerable importance. I engaged in discussions with the principal officers of two of them-Secretary General Van Lennep of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, and Secretary General Luns of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization-and gained from them assessments of the international situation as viewed from their special perspectives, as well as generous acknowledgements of the important contribution made by Canada to each. This opportunity extended, in the case of NATO, to a full working session with the North Atlantic Council in Brussels. I was able there to explore with the permanent representatives of the member countries the concepts enshrined in the Ottawa Declaration of Atlantic Principles and to provide assurance that Canadian commitment to those principles remained unimpaired. I was able as well to express Canada's distress that two NATO allies should be engaged in a dispute with respect to Cyprus, and Canada's interest in seeing an early and peaceful resolution of the conflict on that island, a conflict which has taken two Canadian lives and endangered many others.
A few years ago, Mr. Speaker, an experienced European commentator described Canada as "La derniere chance de l'Europe". It is not my place to comment on that observation. I do say, however, that Europe is une bonne chance, une grande chance, une chance tres importante for Canada. That is why we have so studiously strengthened there our ties and our level of representation in recent years. In each of the cities I visited there are three Canadian embassies devoted to separate tasks, and three Canadian ambassadors of outstanding capabilities. I know, Mr. Speaker, that hon. members will share with me my pride in the accomplishments of all of them and particularly, I
October 28, 1974

am sure, of Canada's Ambassador to Belgium, our ex-colleague and your distinguished predecessor.

speechtext:
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I should be less than gracious if I resumed my seat before paying tribute to the skill and dedication of those who accompanied me and who offered such valuable support in my discussions and negotiations. This group, comprised of the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) and senior officials, functioned superbly. Representing, as they did, both of Canada's official linguistic communities and many regions of our country, these individuals demonstrated to me and to our hosts the advantages and the attainments of a bilingual government. I am proud of them and thank them in your presence.
I have not the slightest doubt that they and their colleagues will function equally as well during the several negotiations about to commence, and in the preparations for my return to Europe early in the new year. On that occasion, too, I trust I shall enjoy once again the pleasure of the company of the person who, without question, is Canada's fairest and foremost representative-my wife.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert L. Stanfield (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: EUROPEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, let me begin my comments on a gracious note by saying how pleased we all are to see the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and Mrs. Trudeau back in Canada after their strenuous journey to Europe. I congratulate the Prime Minister on achieving the impression that this was a working trip. There were no bannisters, bobsleds or bugaloos getting attention on this foray. This in itself is progress. I understand there were attempts to whip up glitter and glamour as to what the trip was intended to accomplish.

subsubtopic: EUROPEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT
speechtext: Weak.

subsubtopic: EUROPEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT
speechtext:
My remarks are bound to be weak, coming after the lofty sentiments expressed by the Prime Minister a few moments ago. As I say, there was an attempt to whip up glamour as to what the trip was intended to accomplish. However, I understand the Prime Minister was pretty cool toward that approach to the extent of shooting down some of the most exuberant members of his entourage. For that I also congratulate him.
I say in all seriousness that it was unfortunate our general presentation, particularly that concerning the European common market, was not as thoroughly prepared as it might have been. It strikes me as strange that weaknesses in our presentation were not spotted, criticized and changed before we were on the firing line with them. The Prime Minister has to be subject to criticism in that regard. This was a highly personalized mission and the homework should have been better done before the fact.

subsubtopic: EUROPEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT
speechtext:
Hear, hear!
European Economic Community

Franco-Canadian relations are of particular significance to our country, both culturally and economically.
Beyond the warm welcome the French government extended to the Prime Minister, the setting up of two study groups in the fields of energy and industrial cooperation constitute tangible proof that our two countries are on the road to reconciliation, making up a seven year old breach.
Still, I deplore the fact that so few efforts were made in the past, and with such deliberation, with a view to taking much greater advantage of the European possibilities as a means of reducing Canada's dependence on foreign countries. I have now for a long time advocated the speedier development of our trade as a means of diversifying our economic relations.

After all, we in Canada have had a lot of time to look at Europe; a lot of time to formulate ideas and approaches. For far too long we neglected the European Economic Community, going along without diplomatic representation assigned specifically to the community. For most of the year 1970 we did not have an ambassador to Brussels or to the community. We created the impression in a good many circles that we were not really interested in the affairs of the European Economic Community. The government has recently made some efforts to correct that impression. The Prime Minister's visit was to be the culmination of those efforts. Therefore, there was a strong challenge to face in this aspect of the Prime Minister's European trip. There was more than ample time properly to prepare to meet the challenge.
I do not for a moment think that the Prime Minister should have been expected to come back with the Holy Grail, or anything like that. I am saying that our preparedness, in terms of presentation, was not up to scratch. With the time we had to prepare a solid case, there is no excuse for having presented something less than that.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: EUROPEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT
speechtext:
The Prime Minister spoke of a return visit to Europe early in the new year. I trust by that time our homework will be better done. There is some very real confusion about just what we were after and just what we were prepared to give in exchange. The Prime Minister's statement today does not clarify the matter to any degree of satisfaction. I hope he will be more frank and forthcoming in answering some questions on these points.
It seems the trip had three main areas of concern. First, to renew warm relations with the government of France. I certainly think this purpose was fully accomplished. Second, to touch base with regard to our commitment to collective security, NATO for example. Because of the Prime Minister's warm support for NATO over the years, there is no need for me to comment on that. Third, to explore possibilities of a contractual arrangement with the European Economic Community.

October 28, 1974
European Economic Community
It is in relation to this third point that most of the confusion exists, and the Prime Minister does not really help to clear the air when he says things like this:
There was a significant meeting of minds on the concept of this new relationship and on the additional steps to set the process in motion.
If there was a significant meeting of minds on the concept, I wish the Prime Minister would tell us what the concept was.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: EUROPEAN ECONOMIC COMMUNITY-STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER ON VISIT
speechtext:
Here is what the Prime Minister says they agreed on. Hon. members should listen to this with great care:
The parties agreed to begin exploratory talks in the near future on the nature and scope of negotiations intended to define the form and content of the relationship between them.
On page four of the Prime Minister's statement the word "posture" is used. It is not a word I would have chosen but perhaps it conveys more than it was intended to convey. I say this because the noun when it is verbalized indicates posturing. I have to say it looks to me like posturing as far as the EEC is concerned. Perhaps the Prime Minister would table the aide memoire sent to the EEC earlier in the year so that we can judge for ourselves.
I am disappointed that the Prime Minister did not take the House into his confidence today. I had hoped for an open review of the intentions of the government toward the EEC-a guide to the kind of association the government of Canada is seeking. We did not get that at all. If the Prime Minister would take this as coming from a native Nova Scotian, all we got today was a bag of fog.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the members of the New Democratic Party wish to join with other members in this chamber in extending a welcome to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on his return from his eventful journey. The trip the Prime Minister made did not produce any spectacular announcements. Nevertheless, the fact that the discussions took place was in itself worthwhile.
At this period in world history when we are faced with inflation on a global scale, when there is growing concern about the diminution of many of our basic natural resources, there is a great danger that many nations will resort to protectionism, a course which can only lead to trade wars. For a country such as Canada which is so dependent upon international trade, such a situation would be abhorrent. For this reason, any discussions in which the Prime Minister takes part with heads of other governments, whether in Europe or elsewhere, must be welcomed. The Prime Minister referred to his discussions with the high officials of the French government. I am somewhat concerned that he would say, on page two of his statement:
One working group will concentrate on examining, without advance commitment, technological and trade investment possibilities with respect to petroleum, gas, coal and nuclear fuels, taking into account matters of interest to both sides.
When one combines this statement with the statement which was attributed to the Prime Minister by the press

while he was in Brussels to the effect that Canada is in the process of reviewing its resource policies, and that those who were interested in the development of resources had better get on the band wagon, it becomes apparent that there is at least some reason for our concern. This, to me, looks like an open invitation-an indication that we are prepared to allow our resources to be used as a bait to attract investment and enlarge our trading opportunities by trading them off in a process of quid pro quo. I want to suggest that this is a dangerous path. We have trodden it particularly in our relations with the United States and it will be no less abhorrent in our relations with Europe. The resources at our disposal in Canada are limited in quantity. Some of them are disappearing rapidly. It is likely we shall face difficult problems in future years, particularly with respect to energy supplies, and for us to suggest we are in a position to invite other countries to come in and share in the development of our petroleum, gas, coal and nuclear fuels will, it seems to me, start a trend for which future generations of Canadians will pay dearly.
On page four of the statement the Prime Minister refers to his discussions with the EEC in Brussels. He says:
We agreed that the dangers of nuclear proliferation demanded the design and implementation of more thorough and effective safeguards.
As to the record, I think all of us would agree. What is needed, however, is some statement from the government, particularly from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) as to any specific safeguards which are being implemented. The safeguards provided in the past have not proved to be effective. In any case, the situation has changed very radically because the by-products of nuclear plants generating electricity can now be used to make nuclear bombs. Consequently, the problem of safeguarding the use of our uranium is more complex than it was a few years ago. I believe the rhetoric of our Prime Minister, the meeting of minds in Brussels in respect of adequate safeguards, is something which ought now to reveal itself in terms of effective regulations so that we can be assured that Canadian uranium, or uranium from any other country if it comes to that, will not be used to enable irresponsible nations to produce atomic weapons which could very well destroy the world.
The Prime Minister is quite right when he says, on page seven of the statement, that it would be irresponsible for a Canadian government not to seek a definitive relationship with the EEC. The fact is that for at least the last ten years members of this party have repeatedly asked successive Liberal ministers of trade and commerce what they were doing with regard to seeking some type of associate membership in the EEC or some trading relationship with that organisation. It is true we were told that some discussions were going on between officials of our Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, the governments of Europe and the EEC, but there had been no attempt until now by the head of a Canadian government, after more than 10 years of having Liberal governments occupy the treasury benches, to reach some agreement with the European Economic Council. If as the Prime Minister says it is irresponsible for a Canadian government not to have sought some distinctive relationship, then the blame for following an irresponsible policy must lie with the gentlemen who sit on the treasury benches.
October 28, 1974

The Prime Minister made some proposals to the EEC when he was in Brussels and press reports have said that the EEC representatives thought the proposals were banal. I should like to know what those proposals were or what type of proposals the government put before the EEC. What are we to envisage? Are we seeking some type of associate membership or are we seeking some type of trade agreement? What are the proposals the government put before them? They are 10 years late in making any kind of proposal, but surely now any proposal ought not to be so meaningless that it is described by the EEC as being banal.
If these proposals are not merely a public relations exercise, surely we ought to know what they are and the reason the members of the EEC were not prepared to accept them. Even though we have been late in recognizing the trade potential of the EEC that is no reason we should not press on now. I hope the government will be much more zealous in pursuing this matter now than it has been in recent years.
As far as this party is concerned I want to say that in pursuing agreements for increased trade it should be made abundantly clear that the natural resources of Canada which we so deeply need and which ought to be processed, and if possible turned into manufactured goods in this country, should not be put up for auction to the multinational corporations of Europe, the United States or anyplace else.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, I must apologize for not having had the time to glance at the statement of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who came back from France in perfect health. Still, I want to congratulate him and join my colleagues in welcoming him back.
The Prime Minister probably came back from France in six or seven hours. As for me, it took me 16 hours and a half to come back from the Lac-Saint-Jean.
Today, the matter of time is very relative over certain distances, since everything depends on the means of transportation. This is the reason why I did not have time to get prepared to answer the Prime Minister's statement.
I simply want to make a few comments on what he has just said as far as the proposed establishment of study groups on economic, trade and technical matters is concerned. I want to express all the happiness we, French Canadians, felt when we read in the newspapers that the Prime Minister of Canada would go to Paris. After waiting for several years, the French speaking people of Canada were glad to read that the Prime Minister would at last meet representatives of the second mother country, in order to renew old friendships. I think that meeting was logical and normal.
Following the Prime Minister's journey through the press, radio and television, I realized that this visit of the Prime Minister of Canada to France was of current interest. It was even eagerly awaited by the French government. Judging by the way the talks developed, I think
House of Commons
everything went well. I hope the proposed working groups will take shape shortly, and that we will be able to say that Canada gets as much from its dealings with France as with Great Britain or any other country.
Today, in its international relations, it is imperative that Canada step up contacts with other countries, increase international agreements in order to lay the old myth to rest, namely that we must always deal first with a North American country. I believe that will be beneficial to Canada. That visit to France has enabled the Prime Minister to open a door to the European Common Market. European trade is developing more and more and I believe that Canada has to be part of it.
The Prime Minister also talked about his visit to NATO. He stated that Canada's contribution to NATO would continue. As for me, I hope that it will get larger, and I believe that all those who have had the opportunity to sit in at NATO conferences will agree with that. I already had the opportunity on three occasions to attend such meetings in Paris and in Brussels, and I realized then the need for such international associations for a country that wishes to play a part in this world and to keep pace with other countries.
I believe that all those agreements are necessary to Canada and 1 hope that this government and the Prime Minister will pursue such conversations with other industrialized countries so as to enable Canada to play a still greater part, so that we may feel more free, more independent and be able to live alongside great industrialized countries without any embarrasment whatsoever.
We are happy to welcome the Prime Minister back and I hope that the talks he has and the contacts he made in Europe will soon bear fruit.

NEWSPAPER COLUMN BY PRIME MINISTER-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to seek leave of the House to propose a motion under the terms of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity arising from the venture into the field of journalism which appeared in the October 23 issue of the Lanark Era and other weeklies in Canada headed "Priorities for the Thirtieth Parliament, Pierre Elliott Trudeau, Prime Minister". Seconded by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) I seek leave to move:
That in the opinion of the House newspaper columns dealing with government policy, which are represented as written by the Prime Minister or by any member of cabinet, but which have actually been written by Liberal Party of Canada employees, constitute misleading the Canadian people, possible manipulation of the press for political purposes and they should cease forthwith.

USE OF TEMPORARY EMPLOYEES AT TAXATION DATA CENTRE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. I am prompted by the recent attempts by the Public Service of Canada to obtain, through newspaper advertisements and householder mailings, thousands of inexperienced temporary employees for the Taxation Data Centre in Ottawa, who will become eligible for unemployment insurance benefits at the end of the peak season. This situation exists, Mr. Speaker, because the Taxation Data Centre is a major employer of keypunch operators in Ottawa and the government has made inadequate attempts to spread the workload over the year or to use experienced people already on unemployment insurance or to disentitle part-time or seasonal workers from unemployment insurance benefits. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Parry-Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Darling)
That this House instruct the departments of National Revenue, Manpower and Immigration, and Finance, to co-operate in devising a method of filling the government's needs for temporary workers without imposing an unemployment insurance burden on the Canadian taxpayers.

maintopic: UIC-BENEFIT ENTITLEMENT FOR PERSONS OVER 70 YEARS OF AGE
speechtext: An insured person ceases to be eligible for regular unemployment insurance benefits from the beginning of the month following the date on which he attains the age of 70 years. The House resumed from Tuesday, October 22, consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet that Bill C-2, to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Bank Act and to repeal an act to amend an act to amend the Combines Investigation Act and the Criminal Code, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take part in the debate on this bill, one which is of vital concern to almost all Canadians whether they recognize it or not. The measure will certainly have a direct effect on a great many small businesses in this country and, though some people may not realize it, it will thus have a great bearing on the interests of consumers. By destroying competition, the legislation which has been brought before us is likely to have a harmful effect upon the future well-being and financial consideration of consumers, despite any short-term benefits which some may think it appears to offer.
This bill has been treated like a dirty shirt by the government. It has grey areas. It might even be referred to as a grey bill. It is moth-eaten, it is worm-infested, and it is an ill-conceived piece of hypocrisy. While the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) may think he has a problem trying to deal with bugs in hamburger, I suggest the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) will have a great deal more to deal with in the future if this bill passes in its present form. In order to describe this measure adequately, small businessmen might have to go to a former president of the United States and ask whether he has any unused expletives to spare.
I think Mr. Speaker should have the authority and the responsibility to order a minister to withdraw a piece of legislation which does not measure up to a certain stand-

ard. The piece of legislation before us today certainly does not measure up. I think it is arrogant of any minister to ask the House to receive legislation which, he says, will be amended during the committee stage. There is no reason why this bill should not be withdrawn. The amendments should be made, and only then should it be returned to the House for second reading. These proposals are not fair to businessmen, they are not fair to the consumers, and they are not fair to the House of Commons. The amendments are of great importance and we should have unlimited time in which to discuss them. Such is not the case during the committee stage, for everyone recognizes that committee members do not have unlimited time in which to enter into debate with the minister or to ask him questions. A question was asked on Friday by my hon. friend from Capilano (Mr. Huntington), as follows:
I have a question for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Further to the request of members from this side of the House on Tuesday of this week that the minister's proposed amendments to Bill C-2 be tabled, would the minister tell us if he now intends to table his amendments, and, if so, when?
The minister replied by saying the amendments would be introduced when the bill was considered in committee. This is not good enough: it is not fair and it is not just. In proposing this legislation, the government is being unfair to Canadians by creating bureaucratic regulations, purporting to be for the benefit of the people, which in the long run will cause more hardship and will ultimately hurt the vast majority of our people including, of course, consumers. I believe the bill to be a farce. No doubt to those who are adherents of socialism, "profit" is a dirty word. In a socialistic country a person does not need to worry about profit because there isn't any for anybody.
I must remind hon. members that, although there are two airlines operating within our borders, they both charge approximately the same rates. Air Canada, the government-owned airline, was the one which first requested permission to increase its rates-and there is no doubt in the mind of any person familiar with these airlines that Canadian Pacific is much more efficient than its competitor and that its service is better.
I believe, and I am confident that most hon. members and all Canadians will agree, that no segment of our society while holding a monopoly should have the right to deliberately gouge our people. There should be some guidelines. But the question is: should the profit margin be determined according to unspecified, arbitrary, government-established councils responsible to no one? When we are faced with a situation of this type, we have to ask ourselves: are we to surmise that all knowledge of industry and business is to be found within the cabinet or government departments? While some individuals in both sectors would perhaps like to give the impression that they have a monopoly on resource knowledge, I for one feel there is a greater supply of ability and know-how within business and industry. In view of this circumstance, why should a profit margin base be created by inexperienced technocrats and bureaucrats?
Mr. Speaker, what is the matter with proper competition? I want to make it abundantly clear, however, that I do not wish to protect the suppliers of the necessities of life at the expense of being unfair to consumers. This will definitely happen if we destroy competition within the
October 28, 1974

business sector. Nothing can take the place of competition, and competition should come from competitive operations and not government restrictions.
I am wondering whether or not the minister has consulted his colleagues in cabinet about the operations of Information Canada. I have here an article which states that a government publication is a best-seller. It suggests that the federal government has a runaway 65-cent best-seller in its latest set of proposals for new business competition law. It goes on to state that this is one set of proposals that may soon be headed for critical review in parliament and in the business community. The reason it is a best-seller is that people in small business are very interested in the bill now before us. I should like to see whether the sales policy of Information Canada can stand up against the regulations in this bill.
Within this government there seems to be a tendency for each minister to set up his own private empire: each one appears to want to operate entirely unto himself. This situation is probably encouraged by bureaucrats who are well entrenched in their departments and have been dictating policy for so long that they are of the opinion it is their right to forge ahead without considering the consequences to this country and its citizens.
Are there to be provisions in this legislation to control government departments? All departments of government must realize their dependence one upon another-and this has to start with the minister. The Prime Minister, as head of the government, should be responsible for co-ordinating uniting programs and policies within all government departments and agencies. The government is not the place within which to construct personal ivory towers, to build egos or to enter a race to surpass another department or its minister.
The government is a body of people who are all public servants whether elected, appointed or placed in office by merit, and unless these employees of the people co-operate and consider the people-who, after all, pay the bills-no single department can efficiently reach its goal or render a useful service. There is a great deal of dissatisfaction among Canadians over the arbitrary action of governments and government departments. As I tried to point out earlier, this is why the book available from Information Canada is being so widely purchased by businessmen.
As was said by the minister, this bill is only windowdressing. When answering questions in this House about the action the government was going to take to allow reasonable profits without deliberately gouging the Canadian people in the area of manufacturing, the Prime Minister's pat answer has always been the same, namely, that the bill now before the House should be passed. How naive can the Prime Minister become, and how misleading is this statement? Does he honestly believe he can tell Canadians in general and members of this House that Bill C-2 will have any positive consequence? Instead of the bill being referred to as the competition bill, it should be referred to as the "get the government off the hook" bill. The only difficulty is that it will not get this government off the hook but will, instead, prove how inadequate government policy is and can be.
Combines Investigation Act
We must realize that at the speed governments function, it will take an extended period-maybe even years-for any action, and in the meantime legitimate business will suffer. I take particularly strong exception to the provision in this bill which allows the commission to make ultimate decisions in respect of prosecution. I have a terrible fear about putting unlimited power into the hands of any individual, no matter who he may be-and I would even include the minister in that statement. I refer to clause 5 of the bill wherein it is provided:
One of the members may be appointed by the governor in council to be vice-chairman of the commission and any member so appointed shall, whenever the chairman is absent or unable to act or whenever there is a vacancy in the office of chairman, exercise the powers and perform the duties of the chairman.
The governor in council may designate a member to exercise the powers and perform the duties of the chairman of the commission whenever the chairman and any vice-chairman are absent or unable to act or whenever the offices of chairman and vice-chairman are vacant.
The clause provides, further, that certain subsections of the act are to be repealed and the following substituted:
Two members constitute a quorum. The commission may make rules for the regulation of its proceedings and the performance of its duties and functions under this act.
This is not the way in which a business should operate. Surely some responsibility should be placed on the government and on the House of Commons to establish a set of regulations that will be acceptable to the Canadian people and will get the required job done. I have faith in the justice of the courts in Canada, but I have doubts about the justice or judgment of some members on the opposite side of this House. Let us consider two government debts, the operations of the CBC and the Canada Council. I suggest neither one of these would establish faith in the minds of Canadians. Many honourable members on the other side of this House were saying, during an election campaign, that the land was strong. I should like to quote some figures about government increased debt including the year 1972.
The national debt of this country has increased rapidly in the last few years. It is my understanding that the increase from 1969 to 1972 was some $12 billion. How can anyone suggest that the land is strong with that kind of increase in our national debt? As was pointed out by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was originally expected to operate on a budget much less than the present cost of that department. The hon. member pointed out that there has been a cost to that department of $450 per phone inquiry and $1,250 per written complaint. I suggest this increase is paid by the consumer, the very person this bill purports to protect. Let us for a moment consider the statements made by members on the other side during the last election campaign. There was a promise in respect of $500 for each new home owner. There was a promise in respect of there being an Air Canada improvement in Winnipeg. Neither of these promises has been kept, and we have heard little or nothing more of them.
This bill is supposed to protect the consumer against false advertising. I am wondering if this government could be charged because of the false promises it has made in order to get elected. What has been done in respect of the

October 28, 1974
Combines Investigation Act
present subsidy on beef? The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) stated that the subsidy on beef would benefit the Canadian people. To the present time there has not been one dollar in the way of subsidy chargeable to the Canadian treasury, and at the present rate there never will be anything paid out under this policy. Catastrophe will have to strike the industry if anything is ever paid out. On top of this, the Minister of Agriculture has egg all over his face as a result of the destruction of some 28 million eggs. The whole situation does not smell too good. But it is useless for him to travel around the country telling the people he is protecting the beef industry, when actually that is not the case.
We find that most of the government's vote-getting promises are not being kept. Could this not be taken as false advertising or misrepresentation? This bill does not allow anyone to use false or misleading advertising. If a private individual or enterprise follows the same pattern, there could be prosecution. But can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, a governor in council appointee as provided for in clause 5 laying a charge against those who appointed him? Let us consider subclause 9 of clause 5: it provides as follows:
The commission may make rules for the regulation of its proceedings and the performance of its duties and functions under this act.
As I said earlier, this House of Commons should ensure that these regulations are spelled out by the highest court in Canada, the House of Commons. This subclause spells out, to me, just one thing. The commission will not be required to take any action if it does not wish to do so; yet it is given devastating power that could be very detrimental to business. What kind of thinking is this? It certainly does not signify a good omen for those who are not in favour of this legislation. Palsy-walsyism is something which Canadians can ill-afford: it is not fair; it is not just; it is not necessary.
I would ask the minister what effect this bill will have on the franchise system that now protects small business and industry. Take, for example, a small Pepsi-Cola plant which employees 10, 12 or 15 people. Such a plant does not mind the competition it receives from another Coca-Cola or any other soft drink plant. But I assure you, Mr. Speaker that if this bill does allow a competitor to move in on it with a like franchise, taking over some of the business, such a company will inevitably go bankrupt; perhaps both, and, as one representative told me, welfare is the next step. So I wonder what the government and this minister are trying to bring about by placing before this House a bill that will have such an effect and does nothing to ensure supply of the product required by the consumer at a low price.
For instance, while one company might have its bottles out on a five-cent deposit, there is nothing to stop a competitor moving in and offering ten cents for the same bottles, because the value of the bottle might be anything between 12 cents and 15 cents. There is nothing in the bill to protect the industry in this way. If the system is destroyed, the result will be higher prices.
The present bill does little to help independent retailers who are being forced out of business by large chains and

department stores. While the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission would be given jurisdiction over supply and sales practices, it would have no power to halt mergers, prevent underselling or any of the means by which large companies and chain stores eliminate their competitors. The minister has indicated that the legislation will be used to regulate the larger corporation and will not interfere with small business. If this is so, the minister should specify what size of corporation or business will be subject to the regulations under the legislation.
An amendment could be introduced to the effect that a business with assets and sales of less than a certain amount could not be said to be engaging in a restrictive trade practice. The question is important, because these people are spending a great deal of money in an effort to protect their interests. They do not know what they are actually up against. They are more or less shadow-boxing and are spending money they can ill afford. This money eventually will have to come from Canadian consumers.
Mr. Speaker, I have asked what is to be done about a political party which does not live up to its promises. Is the individual who made a specific promise to be held responsible, or will the officers of the political party be held responsible? Under the jail sentence provision, upon conviction, in respect of Bill C-2, the present Liberal government, by not fulfilling its election promises, would be faced with deciding whether its leader should be sentenced to jail, or whether the penalty should be paid by a section of the Liberal representatives in the other place who formed a large part of their party's organization in the recent election.
For a moment, Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring to your attention the proposal of the federal take-over of Polymer last year by the CDC. If this corporation should be guilty of an infraction, would an arm of government be prosecuted? These are questions which should be answered in this House rather than in the committee. I have emphasized many times that communication between government departments is almost impossible to detect. I ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) if he is prepared to live with this legislation of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. Is he willing to sell government bonds, under current advertisements, with proclamations of stability and a solid return on investment? The advertising might be fair if inflation were under control, but let us consider what actually happens to those who purchase government savings bonds in good faith. I think I should tell members opposite a fact of which everyone in Canada should be aware, although apparently they are not.
If an individual buys a government bond this year, at the present rate of inflation, in two years' time he will probably suffer a loss of 6 per cent in respect of the value of the bond. He will lose that much in actual net worth, yet the Minister of Finance says government savings bonds represent a stable operation, a stable commitment and a stable investment. We have this legislation which specifies that business must "do as I say, but don't do as I do". This bill is for those who produce, manufacture and develop. It does not apply to those who have the fun of spending-in this case the federal government. I am sure that the people of Canada during the recent election were
October 28, 1974

not aware of the double standard this government was about to foist upon them.
What about large union organizations which rip off their members? Do they give a fair return for dues collected? What about the promises made to non-union employees to entice them to become union members, and what happens to large amounts of membership dues which are siphoned off for the benefit of the hierarchy of union administrations without any thought of return to benefit of their individual memberships? Clause 2 exempts authorized collective bargaining units from the restrictions of this bill. While it may be neither politically, socially nor economically desirable to regulate collective bargaining, unions clearly have an impact on competition and discussion should be initiated on the competitive legitimacy of some of their practices. Large unions are fighting for power and domination over the people.
I have serious doubts about other areas of the bill. There is nothing in this bill to give the consumer, the Canadian people, the protection which is necessary in the most vital area of our economy. While the commission has tremendous power, it is not obliged to consult an accused before prosecution. It should have to advise the respondent of the complaints made, and what are the alternatives. Such, however, is not the case.
It is often the case, when governments introduce complex legislation which has taken ministers and senior public servants months to prepare, that the average person sits back and thinks that these are matters which cannot affect him. But such is not so. This legislation will affect every Canadian. We in the opposition stress as strongly as possible that it is important Canadians know what is incorporated in this bill, and what the consequences might be. Many Canadians adopt the attitude that it does not matter. Although it must be conceded that this is a long and confusing bill, even big businessmen have difficulty in interpreting some of its provisions. It must be taken very seriously, because it involves sweeping changes in business and commercial activity across this country.
This is why I say-and I say it very sincerely-that the minister should have been honest and presented his amendments with the bill; otherwise he should have withdrawn the bill and presented it when it had been amended because, at present, although it has been said that the legislation does not conflict with marketing boards, by the same token the bill provides that an individual cannot withhold anything from the market. This is what marketing is all about, and there is a great deal to be explained to the Canadian people regarding this proposed legislation.
What about the Canadian Wheat Board? Will their selling procedures be considered legitimate? This is not explained in the bill. That is why the minister should rise in this House and state unequivocally what the amendments will be. One such amendment could incorporate legislation which would wipe out all the freedom that has been given to marketing boards, thereby destroying a surety of continuing production of basic products for the benefit of Canadians. The minister may say, "No, we do not intend to do that," but what guarantee do we have that once the legislation is passed and the toe is in the door, the
Combines Investigation Act
Canadian people, the Canadian producer and the Canadian consumer will be protected?
I impress upon the House that we need increased production. While we may have a favourable trade balance, I should like to stress the fact that in 1972, 1973 and 1974 this favourable balance was brought about in respect of exporting our raw materials and basic agricultural products, but in every other area we were down. In no quarter did we export more manufactured products that we imported-and this is where we must build our economy; this is where the jobs are. What is the use of having a product in Canada to sell if we have no purchaser for it? If people do not have the income with which to pay for the product, it is useless to produce it.
The minister has been less than fair in presenting the bill in this form. He would do well to withdraw it and to bring it back in a form acceptable to the House, with the proposed amendments so that we know what we are debating.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time legislation of this type has come before the House, and it will not be the last time I will be critical of it. In my view, no single piece of mythology has been more persistent and more harmful to this country than the continuation of the idea that somehow or other we can solve the defects in our present economy and our market system by legislation dealing with combines or restrictive trade practices. In my view, aside from a few regulating suggestions which appear in the bill-which could be handled by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs without any difficulty- we should abandon such an approach to solving consumer and marketing problems in this country. I would like to give some reasons for saying that.
First, I would have some positive feeling for the legislation if I thought there was any chance that it might work. The evidence is that it has never worked in the past, and there is no real reason to believe it will work in the future. If you look at the number of convictions under the Combines Investigation Act, you will find almost none. There is good reason for this. It is almost impossible to obtain evidence of the kind that is necessary to get a conviction. Usually, when a conviction has been laid it should have been for stupidity, not for collusion, because you have to be very stupid to be convicted under the Combines Investigation Act.
One of the cases that I recall concerned cement, in Windsor. Some people were working in collusion in fixing the price of cement in the area. They kept minutes of the meetings and called in their lawyers because they did not trust each other. That is one way of fighting it. Another case was, I think, in Hull dealing with the construction industry. One firm had a brother-in-law there who made notes of the bids everyone was going to make, and in the course of opening the bids the brother-in-law's little memos fell on the floor. That is about the only kind of case in which you get convictions under the combines legislation. Often, even where it appears to work it does enormous harm to the extent that combines legislation is sometimes a restraint in the wrong way.

October 28, 1974
Combines Investigation Act
I think that the effective harm of the combines legislation is that it prevents our coming to grips with the real problem. It is a kind of camouflage, a pretence, a way of fooling the public and saying, "Oh, yes, we have the situation under control," when in fact nothing is being done, or nothing in fact can be done, with this kind of approach. The real problems continue. The government can say, "We brought in amended combines legislation, so you should be happy." It seems to me that combines legislation is the businessman's best friend. Despite all the crying that the businessman does about combines legislation, in fact he depends upon having legislation of this kind in order to take the heat off him to the extent that nobody will investigate him because, after all, one is protected against shennanigans.
If you ask a minister, in the House, what he is going to do about an instance that arises, such as when today my colleague the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mr. Rodriguez) asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) a question about the pricing of dry milk, the minister says he is sure his officials will consider the matter, and so will people in the combines branch. When? In five, six or a hundred years from now- which is to say never. The point was that an important question was asked in the House and the minister was able to duck it completely because he had the combines legislation to hide behind.
There is nothing in the present bill that will make the situation any better. Without that combines legislation, the minister would have been forced to give a decent answer-at least an answer that he would look at the situation and take some action. If he did not respond effectively within two or three days, there would have been another question until we did receive some kind of answer. At the moment it is shunted off. I am sure he will not get away with it, because the hon. member for Nickel Belt will not let him; but he will certainly make every attempt to pretend that some action will be taken under the Restrictive Trade Practices Act. I am not saying that the minister is doing it deliberately or that he wants to be less than a good minister; I am simply saying that this arrangement enables him, or perhaps forces him, to deal with questions of this type in the way he did.
Years ago we were talking about having a minister of consumer and corporate affairs. It did not look as though we were going to get one, because the government was dreadfully opposed to the idea. But when we finally got one, we said, "We will finally have a minister who will be responsible to the consumer and who will react to problems brought to his or her attention." Instead, all the minister does is shunt these matters on to the restrictive trade practices branch for investigation, which turns out to be no investigation at all.
In many ways, what the businessman does not want is a real inquiry into areas where he has an effective monopoly. Most businessmen do not have an effective monopoly, but there are some who do, and the way they prevent the heat being applied to them is by permitting some small competitors to stay alive so they can turn around and say they have competitors. They may have 95 per cent of the business in that field, but because they have one or two small competitors who live by the good will and acquies-

cence of the giant, they are not subject to investigation. If there were no combines legislation, and if the question of how many businesses are left was not involved, these matters might be investigated.
In 1966, in the food prices committee, we were looking into the price of glass jars for baby food and why baby food had risen in price. It turned out it was because glass jars cost two cents more than the other containers. Nevertheless, they were popular enough that the public was willing to pay. Only two firms, Gerber's and Heinz, were in the baby food industry at that time and both were charging exactly the same for their tinned goods. I found that difficult to understand because Gerber's, which was only in the central market, had 20 per cent of the total market while Heinz had 80 per cent. With 80 per cent of the market, why was it not possible for Heinz to reduce its price? They claimed their costs were not different from Gerber's. That just was not true. When we looked at the financial statements of both companies, it was apparent that Gerber's had been losing money for three years and was in danger of going broke.
Heinz had been using glass jars in the United States for years. When we asked why they were not using them in Canada, they said they did not know what the effect of glass jars would be. When we asked if they did not know about their American operations, they replied that they did not talk to them. But they did know that the consumers wanted glass jars and they knew that Gerber's were going broke. They did not want Gerber's to go broke, so they stayed out of the field for three years until Gerber's could break even. Then they went over to glass jars. That is the kind of competition we have in our society, Mr. Speaker. What we have is price leadership. Who competes with General Motors other than the imports?

speechtext:
Just consider the pricing policies. I remember one occasion when General Motors proposed a price increase and every car manufacturer followed with an equivalent increase. A few days later General Motors said it was a mistake and the increase was $30 too much. Everybody came down by $30. General Motors could drive Ford and Dodge out of business if they wanted to, but they probably would not do it because then somebody would look at their operation. It is more advantageous for a large corporation to keep its competitors alive and to have a little less volume, with more profit. Competition just does not exist in these large markets. General Motors does not have to sit down with Chrysler or the other corporations and suggest making a deal. They just step out and the others follow, because they know if they do not they are in serious trouble. It is "live and let live" in big business. It is not the competitor who is the enemy, but the customer- and combines legislation enables this kind of farce to continue.
In the steel industry, too, one company issues a price list and the other companies follow. There is no proof of collusion because their principals might just have spoxen to each other at the golf club. They would not be stupid enough to sit down with their accountants and keep
October 28, 1974

minutes. Perhaps they do not even talk to each other, but they have ways of signalling.
A society that has modern technology requires large corporations. I am not saying that you could break up General Motors and benefit from it; perhaps the technology of our times requires large firms. Large firms cannot afford to cut each other's throats. They will not fight each other on price; their fight will be on advertising, model changes or gimmicks. The small businessman has no choice but to fight in a kind of suicidal way, but the large corporations have to stick together because the public is their enemy, not their competitors.
I shall make some proposals later about what we could do if we did not have combines legislation, and how we could be protected. Another point about combines legislation, Mr. Speaker, is that it is as American as apple pie. It is not a Canadian idea. It may be pointed out that our combines legislation was introduced a year before the Sherman act in the United States, which is its equivalent. It was introduced with the Sherman act in mind, however. Combines legislation makes a lot of sense in a totally capitalistic society which does not have any ethic of public involvement or public regulation. In that case, you can inject this kind of approach to justify continuance of the sort of tooth and claw attitude that rampant capitalism has as its ethic. If that is why the Sherman act was brought in in the United States, in order to take some rough edges off as somebody on television said about somebody else why do we have to embark on it in an economy where it does not make any sense? The United States is ten or eleven times the size of Canada. This means that in order to attain the same level of efficiency, they can afford ten or 11 times the competition, given the same level of technology.
We should be asking our industries to co-operate, not to collude against the public; to co-operate for purposes of improving efficiency, wages and exports, without having them supervised and regulated by the public. That is the direction in which we should be going. Because we do not want to regulate, we do not want to supervise, and we do not even want to see what they are doing, we bring in something like this combines legislation in the faint hope that it will keep them honest, instead of having public involvement. The only thing that will do any good is public involvement and scrutiny of their activities.
The problem of foreign ownership arises from a number of sources, but one of the chief problems has been the presence of combines legislation which has encouraged the proliferation of branch plants in this country and prevented the normal rationalization of those plants into a Canadian package. I want to talk about famous villains on the Canadian scene. There are two men who have drawn their fair share of attention, and not because they are interested in the public welfare. Perhaps we should not expect big business tycoons to be concerned about that because, after all, that is the responsibility of parliament.
For their own reasons, they put together two industries in Canada which have remained Canadian. They pay high wages, charge low prices to the consumer, and are models in every way. I am sure that these industries were assem-
Combines Investigation Act
bled in direct contravention of the combines legislation. Who are these two fellows? One is Lord Beaverbrook, the other E. P. Taylor. E. P. Taylor amalgamated some isolated beer companies into one of the finest beer producing companies in the world. So efficient is Canadian beer production that the Americans have threatened to pass legislation. This is because they are afraid Canadians will take over their beer industry. I think the government has treated that industry too generously with regard to taxation; but it has remained Canadian, and that is important.
The other industry is steel manufacturing. Ours is one of the most efficient steel industries of the world. Why, Mr. Speaker? I suggest the reason is this; a large number of steelmakers were brought together, probably in direct contravention of combines legislation, because they were threatened by Bethlehem steel and other American steel which was coming to Canada. Lord Beaverbrook, over the heads of Canadian bankers, put together the Steel Company of Canada and established in this country an industry which excels. We can outproduce the Americans in many ways and make steel as fine as theirs, often at lower prices. That industry enjoys little tariff protection. Its workers enjoy parity with similar workers in the United States. Both the industries I have mentioned have remained Canadian; both have been strong enough to withstand foreign ownership.
I do not say Lord Beaverbrook and E. P. Taylor, neither of whom I know, put together these industries from the kindness of their hearts. They are business buccaneers and I am sure their activities should have been regulated. The point is that what they did worked for the benefit of Canada.

speechtext: And for their own benefit.

speechtext:
Quite so. Over-all, their work brought advantage to Canada. I have been invited to meetings of chemical producers. Whenever they hold a convention or want to lobby here once a year, they invite people to address them. The chemical industry is well represented in my riding and I am interested in what goes on. I have talked to people in that industry. The conversation goes something like this. I say, "You guys are pretty inefficient. You have far too many plants trying to serve the market. You have almost as many branches in Canada as in the United States, and you are so inefficient that you need to be protected by tariffs; you go to the government for help." I think the Canadian market is big enough to support the production of many chemicals. That is why I say to these people, "Wouldn't it be better if you all got together?" After all, Mr. Speaker, the idea is not new. It has been tried in Germany. The British are amalgamating their industries. In some cases they come under private ownership, in some cases under public. Personally, I prefer public ownership.
The Swedes have not introduced combines legislation. They have rationalization boards which sit down with Swedish industries and try to make them more competitive in their own and world markets. Canada and the United States are probably the last countries in the world to support combines legislation. If the Americans want to be foolish, should we follow? Too often we have followed that pattern. I suggest it is time to break it.
806

October 28, 1974
