Let me return to my conversations with chemical producers. When I say, "Why don't you people get together," they say, "We can't, because of the combines legislation." The truth is that if they want to get together, they will find a way to do it, combines legislation or not. The point is, they do not want to get together. They argue that if they do, they will be prosecuted in the United States under the Sherman act which has extraterritorial application. As these companies operate internationally, they will not do something in Canada which they are not prepared to do anywhere else in the world. They are integrated. If they co-operate with the government, they do it for their own reasons-not because such co-operation is beneficial for Canada. Such co-operation may disrupt their international actions. This situation is now changing. But for years combines legislation was used as an excuse for maintaining in this country one of the most inefficient industrial structures of the world.
We are worried about the high level of foreign ownership. Do people not realize that foreign ownership has a direct relationship to combines legislation? What can be done in the absence of combines legislation. First, we can adopt the recommendations of the MacQuarrie commission report. On page 16 of the bill, in proposed section 31.2, there is reference to tariffs, a matter covered by that commission. This proposal has been outstanding for almost 30 years. I am referring to the recommendation that those convicted of collusion or conspiring against the public interest should have their tariff protection removed. Mr. Speaker, this protection, so far as I know, has not been removed in a single instance-neither in the case of the glass industry nor the paper industry. These industries have continued in their own merry way. What is the biggest fine which has been handed down under our combines legislation?

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext: Twenty-five dollars.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext: It is a little more than that.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext: I think it's about $50,000.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
If it is $50,000, the fine represents a licence. In no instance has tariff protection been removed. Industry does not worry about a fine, because that can be recovered by increases in price. The government has the weapon but has not used it.
Neither has the government tried another approach. My remarks maybe pertinent to Petrocan; I do not know. Let me refer to what the Swedes have done under their co-ops. Swedish co-ops operate upon a different basis from Canadian co-ops. They go into the market with the specific purpose of driving down prices. If a manufacturer is taking too much from the market, instead of legislating the Swedes permit a co-op to compete with the manufacturer and drive down prices. That is what we should do. A lesson like that would not be lost on those who are raising prices unfairly. If prices are reduced under a system like that, the consumer cannot be asked to make up the difference. But the government is not prepared to do this; instead, it has brought in combines legislation which is meaningless. It is not interested in providing competition through the public sector. This is the area the government should enter.

There is the question of public ownership. If someone abuses this country in terms of ripping off the people, I see no reason why somebody should not step in and say, "Look, buddies; you are behaving very badly"-you always say "buddies" because you want to be nice about it-"and we think we will take you under public ownership. Here is your money; go home." Even if there were an indication the government would do something like that, it would be enough.
I would not want to see the government rush into public ownership at every point of contention. That is not what I am suggesting. However, if the manufacturers in this country, particularly those that are foreign-owned, had any indication that the government of Canada was prepared to take them over if they misbehaved, they would not misbehave. However, as long as there are pussycats there, the companies will go along doing what they are doing.
I want to deal with some of the provisions of this bill. Over the years my party has supported combines legislation because we have felt it is at least something. Perhaps we will do so again. Today I am voicing my own reservations. There comes a time when you have to stop being satisfied with these little tinkerings and do-nothings. Perhaps the time has come for us to call the legislation what it is. There is a clause in the bill on misleading advertising. The government is going to try to define misleading advertising. There will be penalties. A clause which provides it will be applied only to misleading advertising carries the same contradiction as talking about a virgin whore.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext: Explain.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext: What is wrong with advertising? It is not that it is misleading. It is that in many cases it is wasteful and immoral. People do not have to be huckstered into everything. They do not have to be pushed into consumption, consumption, consumption and have such huckstering subsidized by the tax system. The reason there is so much advertising is that 50 per cent of it is paid by the government, so why not spend all kinds of money on it? What is accomplished by having a clause on misleading advertising? It is not that the stuff in the spray can will not take the odour away from your armpit. I am sure it will. What is lewd is that they picture a world full of people judging each other by the smell of their armpits. The idea is how you smell.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext: That is racist.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
I would love to raise a discussion about what one sees on television. You see a picture of a charming girl, with marvellous teeth and a lovely personality. You see a boy look at her and then turn away in disgust: she has not used her underarm deodorant. A thousand years from now people will wonder what kind of a civilization we had, and whether this type of advertising represented our system of values. I do not think this misleading advertising clause will lead to very much. The advertising will become a little more sophisticated. It will be necessary to use real glass instead of artificial glass. A man will have to use his own razor blade instead of someone elses.
October 28, 1974

It will not accomplish anything. Misleading advertising is not the problem in our society.
There is also a clause on double-ticketing. The chief consequence of legislation saying you cannot double-ticket will be that the product is taken into the back room. Double-ticketing can now be done right on the shelf. In future the storekeeper will be put to extra trouble; it will be necessary to take the product into the back room. It will be done a little more neatly, similar to the way in which cattle brands are changed with branding-irons out west. The storekeeper may have to charge three or four cents more because the "3" will not turn into a "5". He must change it to an "8" to make it look better. That is not why food is so high in cost. When this happens, it is an abuse but it does not solve any basic problem in the way we distribute food. It does not solve the problem of overbuilding supermarkets and adding charges on to charges with the kind of merchandising methods we use. That is what we should really be looking at. I quote clause 38(1), found on page 38;
No person who is engaged in the business of producing or supplying a product or who has the exclusive rights and privileges conferred by a patent, trade mark, copyright or registered industrial design shall, directly or indirectly,
(a) by agreement, threat, promise or any like means, attempt to
influence upward, or to discourage the reduction of, the price-
How can you prove that? We have tried before to include something about price maintenance. We have never succeeded. There is no way in which you can succeed. There is no need for that clause, because in many cases it is now being done. Someone discounts a job lot of a brand name product. By cutting the price, he creates all kinds of commotion. The same situation prevails. I presume this is supposed to be for the benefit of small businessmen. We do not have to worry about them. They have so much competition now that they do not know what to do with it. In fact, it is only the small businessman who has to compete; the large corporations do not have to do so.
I sometimes wonder why people stay in small business, considering the hours they have to put in and the knowledge they require in order to run a business. No one is going to tell them you have freed up the market for them. Unfortunately, the market is much too free for them. We can see the consequences of that situation. If you want to see good working conditions and good wages, look at big industry, not small business. Small business cannot afford such luxuries because of the situation in which they find themselves.
This bill attempts to do something about suggested retail prices. It does not say you cannot put on a suggested retail price. If someone wants to sell below that, he can. If he does that now, he can probably get away with it. No piece of legislation will really protect him. Let us take the example of someone who wants to sell below the suggested retail price. The law says the supplier must continue supplying him. Anyone with any practical experience knows what will happen. The supplier will suddenly decide he cannot produce enough to satisfy everyone. Either this person will receive a very low priority, his shipment will end up halfway across the country when he needs it for Christmas, or he will receive blue shirts when he orders grey. There are a dozen different ways to get the
Combines Investigation Act
message across quickly that if you cut the price, you will be in trouble.
If you want effective competition, you must do it in some other way. If a manufacturer has built up his brand and is able to impose the kind of coercion that he does, it is because we have enabled him, through the tax system, to build up a brand name which has a monopoly. It is the monopoly, not the suggested retail price, that creates the problem. The man who has access to the monopoly is usually prepared to do what he is told. Indeed, that is probably what he wants to do; he is happy to see the manufacturer put on a standard price because it also protects him from his competitors.
These are some of the reservations which occur to me. I understand that the co-ops are looking forward to the legislation because proposed section 31.2 has something to do with refusal to deal. I do not believe this section will really force a manufacturer to sell to everyone, because there is a little word in here which could make a great deal of difference. It says a supplier has to sell if a buyer is willing to meet the usual trade terms of the supplier in respect of payment, units of purchase and "otherwise". What is covered by those words "and otherwise"? There are so many loopholes. And this one in particular is like a barn door. Suppose a supplier sells to only one store in a town. Is it suggested that he should be forced by legislation to sell to two, or more? I should be surprised if that were the case, since the effect of the section would then be to tell the manufacturers how to run their businesses.
Is it intended that the act should force manufacturers to sell to a particular store whether they want to or not? Are the Liberals ready to curtail economic freedom to that extent? I do not see how these provisions will work. Suppose a manufacturer says his policy is to sell only to "classy" stores and is withholding supplies simply because a prospective purchaser is running a "hole in the wall"? Will the manufacturer be forced to sell to such a store whether he wants to or not? There is also the suggestion that if one supplier refuses to deliver, a purchaser can go to someone else who will be obliged to deliver. I do not know who wrote this legislation. Perhaps the draftsmen are very good in the academic field or in the public service, but I do not believe they have had much experience in business. I doubt whether the legislation will be of much practical value either to the consumer or to small business.

speechtext:
I am glad the minister has put it forward. More and more Canadian consumers are becoming aware that they need to be protected by legislation against unethical business practices, and it is our duty to listen to the complaints which are coming forward and to act to protect consumers, by legislation if necessary.
I should like to draw attention to the clause which relates to misleading advertising. Clause 36 recommends certain changes thought necessary to protect consumers. I should like to point out that there is an area involving deceitful practices which is not covered by this clause. By way of example, I refer to an advertisement which was used last year to promote the sale of a children's toy. The advertisement in question was aired on CFCF-TV in Montreal in November and December of 1973, having been cleared for use by the Canadian Advertising Advisory Board, a self-regulatory body of the advertising industry and Canadian broadcasting.
The advertisement embodied a technique which was intended to influence consumers, in this case children, to purchase a product without their being aware they were being influenced. The exhortive phrase "Get it" had been inserted four times in a 60-second commercial, in varied lengths of up to one-quarter of a second. The message was too short to be perceived by the rational, conscious mind.
This technique is, I understand, similar to that reputed to be used for brainwashing. I suggest this type of technique is not acceptable to hon. members who sit in this chamber, and it should be banned by parliament. It is generally called subliminal, because the appeal to purchase is made to the potential consumer below his threshold of awareness. I intend to propose an amendment to Bill C-2, proposed section 36(1), when it is studied by the standing committee, should I have the opportunity. Subclause (1) of proposed section 36 presently reads:
No person shall, for the purpose of promoting, directly or indirectly, the supply or use of a product or for the purpose of promoting, directly or indirectly, any business interest, by any means whatever-
I propose inserting paragraph (e), which would read:
-make a representation in an advertisement which contains any technical device which, by using images of very brief duration or by any other similar means, exploits the possibility of conveying a message to, or otherwise influencing the minds of consumers without their being aware, or fully aware, of what has been done.

I believe so. I believe this amendment will receive general support. I have discovered that this tech-

nique is reported to be used widely in the production of television and other advertising. I hope the committee will entertain the suggestion to call professional and technical witnesses who can give evidence to this effect. The advertisement to which I have referred was "discovered"-I put that word in quotation marks-by the Canadian Advertising Advisory Board and this discovery was made public on August 21, 1974, through a press release issued by the Canadian Association of Broadcasters.
No mention was made in the news release of the fact that the advertisement had actually been used. I found that it had been used, and also that it was banned only after the relevant contract had expired and the advertisement was no longer being televised. It was judged as containing subliminal content by the Canadian Association of Broadcasters, the Canadian Radio-Television Commission, the Canadian Advertising Advisory Council in Canada, by the National Association of Broadcasters, the Federal Trade Commission and the Federal Communications Commission in the United States.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ROYAL COMMISSION STUDY TO IMPROVE SAFETY OF PASSENGERS AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should study the advisability of establishing a Royal Commission on the notable shortcomings of Canadian railways and in particular CNR to increase the protection of the public in general and that of the employees in particular and to eliminate accidents and derailments of freight or passenger trains.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on several occasions during the last year and the previous one I asked under Standing Order 43 of the House of Commons that an investigation be made on the operations of Canadian railways and in particular of the CNR.
I would ask hon. members, and particularly those who have seen the big cars go by before, to lend an attentive ear in the few minutes available to me so that I may explain to them the reason for my request.
Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, I noted the numerous railway accidents, mainly derailments, across Canada. As a member for a riding which was more particularly affected and on several occasions by those numerous derailments, it is my duty to ask the House that a royal commission inquire into the management of railway companies, especially the CNR, in order to find the means to cope with the disadvantages of the shocking deterioration of this indispensable service of national interest.
Madam Speaker, we must know the cause of those disadvantages so that we may use that information and every governmental facility to remedy the situation. Moreover, we must try and find new ideas in order to meet not only the requirements but also the wishes of the Canadian people.
I should now like to make a few general remarks with regard to railway safety which is most unsatisfactory in some regions.
In the constituency of Rimouski which I have the pleasure and honour to represent, thousands of people have witnessed numerous derailments in the last few years. Here are a few examples.
Last year, a freight car went off the tracks in the Mont-Joli station and wrecked part of the station.
Some 75 miles from Mont-Joli, in the Matapedia valley, 24 cars carrying oil and various freight also went off the tracks in Routhierville.
The same year, between Mont-Joli and Rimouski, another derailment took place, involving this time passen-
Railway Safety
ger cars. Several cars, including the locomotive, ran off the line between Mont-Joli and Luceville. Fortunately, no one was fatally injured, but those cars lying in the fields were nevertheless a sorry sight.
Madam Speaker, I take this opportunity to inform the House that the traffic in Mont-Joli station is quite heavy owing to the operation about two miles away of a Price Brothers sawmill. All its lumber is shipped by railway, especially the Canadian National, as this is the only line in operation in the whole area.
The accidents which I referred to are quite important. They are very costly when we consider the number of CNR trains and derailments in Canada during 1972. The number of derailments and track breakage has tripled since 1959 and almost doubled since 1969.
It is obvious that one of the main reasons for those accidents and likely the worst, that is the railways do not maintain their trackage properly.
Madam Speaker, the government must make sure that the railways take their responsibilities and carry out their duties. In view of the fact that Canadians have given to them millions of dollars in subsidies, they should be made aware of the way the money made available to the railways is spent.
That is the reason why the CNR must be the subject of a thorough investigation and action must be taken so that the needs and aspirations of all Canadians can be met more adequately.
For a long time, Canadians, businessmen, officials and employees were proud of their railways. Today I note Madam Speaker that, instead of having a very futurist railway system, the CNR has a very deteriorated system and could not ensure the maintenance of neither their trackage nor their rolling stock.
Madam Speaker, I remember accidents used to be a rare occurrence, since maintenance was very good and the ballast rested on cinder. We now have the best ballast, that is crushed stone. But there is no sufficient inspection of broken rails or defective sleepers, and that is the reason for a good number of accidents.
As I said, four employees used to handle the inspection and maintenance of seven miles of trackage. Inspections were then made daily, and often after the passing of various passenger or freight trains. But now, it was deemed adequate to lengthen such sections to 20 miles approximately, while making sure to reduce track inspection and maintenance personnel.
There certainly exists mismanagement within CNR, considering that in order to replace say a window pane at the Rimouski station, one sends for an employee in Camp-bellton, approximately 150 miles away, in order to do the work.
This entails too much undue expense and blatant waste. So do indeed Canadian National executives. I was informed these people use automobiles belonging to Canadian National Railways, and also credit cards with unlimited credit. Such automobiles they use all year long, for the minimal cost to themselves of $50. Few members in this House are allowed such a bargain. As far as I am concerned, I would indeed sell my car in order to use one

October 28, 1974
Railway Safety
supplied by the government, if I had only $50 a year to pay to use it.
It is then easy to understand why Canadian National Railways' debt is around $1.8 billion, with notes bearing interest at 5 per cent. Nonetheless, Canadian National Railways, with assets of $4 billion, has an annual deficit around 25 millions.
Rather than engaging in subsidiary ventures as the building of towers, the developing of shopping centers and property such as luxury hotels, we should first and foremost secure assurance that railway facilities and services are satisfactory and that there are enough cars and locomotives in service.
A thorough inquiry by a royal commission would perhaps enable us to find out what are the failings of the present administration and to correct them.
Madam Speaker, it is important to be able to distinguish accidental and localized faults from fundamental, structural and characteristic defects which would necessitate a complete upheaval and reorganization.
This is a very important matter that requires our full attention and all our energy, if we want to keep in touch with present and future needs and, by the same token, to restore the international reputation and prestige our railways enjoyed in the past.
If the Transport Commission deemed it necessary to recommend to the Canadian National Railways they reduce the speed of their trains to 40 miles an hour, limit the loads and inspect the rails better, all year long, it was so there would be as few accidents as possible on those tracks. Those recommendations are in agreement with the purpose of my motion which is to find solutions to those many derailments.
The Transport Commission must bring pressure to bear, supervise and control, in order to see that the railways have an efficient and adequate rolling stock, take good care of their platforms and also take all necessary steps to provide a proper service for the people of Canada. Otherwise, the railways will keep on disregarding public safety. Transportation is an essential field in which we must develop better policies in the best interests of the national economy.
I feel that in some cases, this government has failed to use the powers granted to it under the act to bring in the necessary remedial measures. Under the actual system, I firmly believe that the CNR is not sufficiently responsible to Parliament. Therefore, I suggest, Madam Speaker, that steps should be taken in this regard.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ROYAL COMMISSION STUDY TO IMPROVE SAFETY OF PASSENGERS AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at the outset may I say I support the spirit and thrust of the motion presented by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard) to the extent that it recognizes the necessity to bring about a greater degree of safety and protection for passengers and employees in connection with Canada's railway system. I am not sure, however, I agree with the hon. member's proposal to establish a royal commission or inquiry.

It seems to me there have been sufficient studies in this particular area and that another study would merely prolong the issue. There are been innumerable studies. One in particular is the report by the Railway Transport Committee on the Canadian Transport Commission. This adequately spells out the shortcomings of the railways in terms of maintaining adequate safety standards.
I believe it is firmly established in our minds, and in the minds of the members of the public, that Canada's railway system enjoys something less than a commendable safety record. This is obvious from the increasing frequency of accidents. In the Third Report of the Transport Committee released in December, 1973, it is indicated that the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific Railways in 1972 had three times as many accidents as in 1959, and nearly double the number in 1969. The explanation by the railways is that they have been moving much more tonnage and that their freight capacity has increased tremendously.
We do not find the airlines using a similar argument. Their safety record has been very high, notwithstanding the fact that they have increased the movement of passengers and cargo by air transport. I do not think we should accept that particular argument of the railway companies. The annual report of the CTC also indicates that an innumerable number of accidents have occurred.
For example, at page 9, the 1973 report of the CTC states:
District officers investigated 296 derailments and 58 collisions between trains. Four persons were killed and 252 injured in such accidents.
It goes on to give the breakdown. I do not believe further studies are required. I do not think that there is need for a royal commission. What is needed is government leadership and action in this area. The general inquiry launched in 1970 dealt quite extensively with trackage roadbed, with the maintenance of trackage, and with signal systems and slide detector fences. Approximately
6,000	pages of evidence were compiled.
That report is available to members and to the public. It was prepared for the Railway Transport Committee and, in my opinion, constitutes a damning indictment of the safety record of the railways. Perhaps I might quote again from that report, at page one of appendix 3 where it states:
The number of derailments caused by track conditions on Canadian National and Canadian Pacific in 1972 is three times that in 1959 and nearly double that in 1969. Because of this continuing increase in derailments to date, it must be concluded that in the foreseeable future the number of derailments on account of track conditions will continue to increase with a continuing increase in the number of injuries and deaths as a result, unless immediate action is taken.
This is a pretty clear indication that the safety record is less than satisfactory. It is also evidence that something must be done immediately.
Furthermore, the report sets forth some positive recommendations and steps which could be followed during the interim period until such time as necessary, longer term, corrective measures are carried out. For example, we know from the report that current stress on trackage is beyond tolerable limits. In this regard we see a specific recommendation put forward by the Railway Transport Committee.
October 28, 1974

I quote again from appendix 3, page 1, as follows:
Until such time as improvements are completed to strengthen the total track structure, it is obvious that the only way in which an immediate reduction in these derailments can be accomplished is to eliminate the overstressing of the existing track structure; that is, reduction of axle loadings. Therefore, since it is the duty of the Canadian Transport Commission to ensure that derailments on account of track conditions causing injuries and deaths be prevented, it will be necessary to require the railways under its jurisdiction to reduce the maximum net weight of carloads to 70 or 80 tons per car and to require the railways to reduce the height of high loads which now result in excessive lateral stresses, and to require the railways to reduce the speed of trains wherever the existing speeds are contributing to excessive stresses beyond the limit for which the present track structure was designed and is being maintained, unless improved programs and standards of track maintenance are immediately undertaken to eliminate the causes of such derailments.
So here again the steps that must be taken to correct and improve safety standards are clearly outlined in this report. We know that in terms of inspections, our lines have not been inspected on a frequent and regular basis. In this regard we might refer to page 5 of appendix 3 of the Third Report of the Railway Transport Committee, which states:
More frequent inspection of track would very often result in the observance of conditions of this type developing which might cause derailments. If more staff, material and equipment were available, more prompt action could be taken to correct these conditions as they are developing and before they could result in derailments. In other words, more frequent inspections by qualified staff and more and better maintenance of track conditions would undoubtedly reduce the number of derailments in this category which so frequently result in personal injury and deaths.
More frequent inspection would also result in observation of the development of other conditions, such as defective switches, conditions leading up to washouts and sunkinks, which would permit prompt corrective action to be taken and thus avoid the possibility of derailments as a result.
The report goes on to make recommendations and suggestions dealing with broken rails, which suggest the necessity of railways acquiring more sophisticated track testing equipment. We know what the problem is, and we know that the condition of the trackage has deteriorated to a standard which is far below that which can accommodate safely the loads which our present day boxcars are carrying. This has an effect on the over-all efficiency of the railways as well as on their safety performance. We know that in order to overcome this, a great deal of money will have to be spent. So what we need now is not a royal commission but government action and government leadership to compel the railways to honour the recommendations and conclusions in the report of the Railway Transport Committee.
Above all, we need a commitment from the federal government to work out some sort of agreement with the railways to provide the necessary funding for this very expensive undertaking. It seems to me that the government has been conspicuously silent on this report, notwithstanding the fact that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) has been questioned on it in the House on many occasions. The only answer we can elicit from him is that he is discussing this matter with the railways, discussions which to date have led to nothing more than simple meetings. The minister's evasive and flippant answers can
Railway Safety
only lead us to believe that very little progress will be made so long as he is minister.
The CNR has indicated that in order to improve trackage to meet current requirements and the current projections of freight and payloads, something in the order of $5 billion will have to be spent over the next six year period. Our railways should be considered as a national asset and, if that is so, it behooves the government to take responsible leadership in this area.
The obligation of the government is clearly outlined in the National Transportation Act and in the Railway Act. The government has the power to compel the railways to maintain a safe and efficient railroad system. If the railways are short of funds, and since they are a vital asset, meaningful discussions should take place in an active way now to bring about a realistic program to upgrade our trackage and our roadbeds to meet our current requirements.
Furthermore, in addition to the infusion of funds and the requirement for a responsible and responsive government leadership, we need full public disclosure of all reports in connection with railroad accidents. In my opinion, the efficiency and safety of the railways is certainly a matter of public interest and public concern. That being the case, it follows that the public has the right to know what is going on in this important and vital area.
So, while I share the thrust and spirit of the motion put forward by the hon. member for Rimouski, I must say that I do not believe that we need a royal commission. I believe that we have sufficient facts and details before us to act upon them, and indeed to correct the substandard levels of operation and maintenance of railroading in Canada. It is not necessary at present to give the government something further behind which to hide. It has a clear responsibility and I urge it to act now. For this government talk is cheap at election time, but I tell its members that actions speak louder than words.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ROYAL COMMISSION STUDY TO IMPROVE SAFETY OF PASSENGERS AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I will only intervene in this debate for a few minutes, because almost everything that can be said on the motion has been said by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard), and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski), and I agree with almost everything they have said on the matter.
I was hoping that the hon. member for Vegreville would go slightly farther than he has been prone to do in the past toward a solution of this problem, among many others, in our transportation industry. The hon. member was correct when he said that the CTC has reported fully in the area of safety, regarding track maintenance, rolling stock and other kinds of equipment and facilities, but the government has not acted to any great extent. The CTC required implementation of some of its recommendations, but action to date has been totally insufficient.
May I say here that while there is a great deal to be critical about with regard to railways operations, the railways are still one of the safest ways to move people or goods, but at the rate railway accidents have increased, they will not keep up this good reputation. Since there is so little excuse for the increase in accident rates, it is

October 28, 1974
Railway Safety
incumbent on the government to require the railways to do better.
I wonder why the hon. member for Rimouski picked on the CNR. If he looked deeply enough he would find the CPR to be just as bad. Neither of them has anything to be proud of in the area about which the hon. member is complaining. In the whole area of track maintenance the railroads have done an abysmally bad job since the early 1960's. One has only to observe the ground from an aeroplane or a helicopter to see literally thousands of miles of trackage which still uses 65 and 85 pound rails made in 1910 or 1911, ties that are replaced at a rate of one third less than had been the practice previously, tracks grown over with weeds, and rails replaced with pieces of other rails once they are broken.
It is not unusual for maintenance and way crews to look after 40 miles of track, and I suggest much of that inspection is done by railway trucks running up and down the highway, parallel to the track.
When I worked for the railway the condition of the tracks was a matter of pride with the section foreman. He went over his track at least once a day, certainly prior to and after a train moving over it. He knew it like the back of his hand. I am not suggesting that crews today should look after five or six miles of track, but I am sure even with 15 or 16 miles to a crew it could be maintained and inspected.
Every year we get complaints from railway employees about lay-offs on rip tracks where small repairs to cars are done, or about lay-offs in railway repair shops. I believe that both railway companies are trying to get by on the cheap, and have reduced their priorities in regard to equipment, repair and maintenance. There has been evidence of understaffing for many years in maintenance and inspection of tracks and equipment.
Because of the railways' involvement in other enterprises there has been no increase in the budget for updating and maintenance of equipment and track. The hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard) mentioned the luxury hotels, the office buildings, apartment blocks and needles in which hundreds of millions of dollars have been invested while the railroads have deteriorated. The government has all the evidence it needs to deal with this problem. It has the authority, and if it needs any further authority it would be surprised at how quickly legislation would go through.
The government should look at transportation systems in the European countries on both sides of the iron curtain, and in Australia and Japan. All modes of transportation are treated as a public utility, owned, operated and regulated by a sort of public utilities board in these countries. Because of this they are operated as public utilities and they have to be maintained and kept up to date in the way that our municipalities control sewer and water systems, streets and sidewalks. Of course that may vary with the city. Some streets in the city of Ottawa look as if they are in the hands of private enterprise.
Publicly owned transportation systems get the priority they deserve. In our country, with its geography, climate and its widely scattered population, we should get rid of

nineteenth century concepts in transportation. Our transportation needs today would be best fulfilled by a publicly owned and operated system. A system that is in the hands of the public would be more responsive to the public and to the needs of the economy, would provide adequate rail and other transportation, and certainly would be adequately maintained and updated.
It should not be necessary year after year for us to be concerned with something so obvious as the necessity of maintaining and updating plant and equipment. It is even being suggested now that the government should take over the road beds. I am sure the CPR would be happy about that, because they have deteriorated to the point that it would cost hundreds of millions of dollars to bring them up to standard. It would just be another way of bailing out the CPR. The government should tell the railroads to give a higher priority to capital expenditures on equipment, trackage, staff and inspection so that accidents and derailments can be reduced in number.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cliff Mclsaac (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ROYAL COMMISSION STUDY TO IMPROVE SAFETY OF PASSENGERS AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard) who moved the motion has raised a matter that is of concern to all members of this House. I know it is of concern to western members because of the miles of track that go through that part of the country.
I was impressed with the argument put forward by the hon. member. In my part of Saskatchewan there have been several fairly major derailments in the last two or three years. I agree in principle with the point made by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski). The way to improve the safety performance of the railroads is not to appoint a royal commission, as the hon. member for Rimouski suggests, although there have been some tremendous ones in the past. The MacPherson Royal Commission looked into the question of railroads, and the Glassco Commission into government operations. They took a long time to prepare their reports. Royal commission recommendations are seldom implemented, because governments tend to put those reports on the shelves to gather dust, perhaps not intentionally.
I suggest that few royal commission recommendations are ever included in legislation or regulations. If they are included, usually this happens some years after a report is brought down. For that reason, I do not think that appointing a royal commission would expedite what the hon. member suggests in his motion, which reads:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should study the advisability of establishing a Royal Commission on the notable shortcomings of Canadian railways and in particular CNR to increase the protection of the public in general and that of the employees in particular and to eliminate accidents and derailments of freight or passenger trains.
May I put on record figures relating to accidents over the past few years. The hon. member for Vegreville said that there has been a threefold increase in accidents and derailments but did not say what was his comparison base. According to figures provided to me, train derailments in 1970 totalled 276, in 1971, 265, in 1972, 323 and in 1973, 299. The increase has been slight, but not dramatic. Accidents
October 28, 1974

involving car collisions and derailments totalled 53 in 1970, 66 in 1971, 76 in 1972 and 72 in 1973. The total number of accidents involving railroads as reported to the CBTC for 1970, 1971, 1972 and 1973 were 4,622, 4,721, 4,818 and 4,688 respectively. I know that such statistics do not mean much, but the mere fact they exist indicates we have a job to do with regard to safety.
I must point out that as our railways have been carrying more and more goods, the number of derailments has not increased to an alarming extent. As the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) said, if you look at what is happening in other modes of transport available for the movement of material you see that the record of the railways is very good. I suggest, therefore, that the route of the royal commission, which many governments have followed in the past, is not the route which the government ought to follow in this regard. It takes a long time before we see any benefit. I suggest it would be better to implement the recommendations which came out of the 1970 study.
We must make certain there is a good working relationship between the railway safety committee, which includes representations of unions, and the CTC and MOT officials. That route should be followed in order to ensure railway safety.
The government has chosen to go through a continuing process of improvement. Possibly in some areas the improvement is not as great as it might be. Many millions of dollars must be found to renew rail beds and ensure that goods carried by the railways are carried with greater safety. To this end the government provided money for the purchase of hopper cars used in the movement of grain. Unfortunately these cars cannot be loaded fully on all lines. That shows that we must upgrade the quality of our road beds so that we may use to the fullest extent these cars carrying grain and other commodities.
More money is to be available for CN capital acquisitions and for the upgrading of lines. Also, we need a railway monitoring system to identify specific problems as they arise, and to recommend solutions. The railways are meeting with shippers. Several studies are under way; they were initiated because of the Western Economic Opportunities Conference. The reports will be made available to the WEOC committee, some by the end of this year, and one early next year. They will deal with the condition of road beds across the west, primarily.
We are continuing our consultations with other provinces, as well as with the western provinces, on matters of this kind. As hon. members know, we are revising old policies and developing new policies in this area, as mentioned in the Speech from the Throne. Without doubt, the job ahead of us is very big. It is one we must do if we are to make progress and go forward.
The government intends to influence and improve general railroad operations. 1 think the allegation made by the hon. member for Rimouski that the CNR does not perform as well as other railways is not borne out by evidence. I suggest that the CNR performs as well or as poorly- whichever way you want it-as any other railway. I could not help noting that the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre included the CPR in his criticism. There is no
Railway Safety
reason why that company should not be included in this discussion.
Improvements have been and are being made in the CN system as a result of maintenance and other work carried out this year by CN. This will include the installation of 1,260 kilometres of new rail, which was more than was laid last year and the year before. In order to improve safety and capacity, CN is installing new signalling and communication facilities. Radio communications are being steadily improved. CN has been active in the search for and development of new techniques for several years, is seeking solutions for its own operating problems, and is involved in joint programs with the Department of Transport and CPR.
I assure the hon. member who moved the motion that the CNR reacts well to general government policies and is continuing to search for solutions to improve the safety of its operations.
In accordance with the duties imposed on the CTC by the Railway Act and the National Transportation Act, the commission is obliged to ensure that all railway operations in Canada are carried out in maximum safety. In order to isolate and identify factors involved in railway accidents and explore the effect on safety of the operation of longer and heavier trains, the commission undertook an inquiry into railway safety in 1970. Perhaps other hon. members are more familiar with it than I am. Some hon. members may have been involved in that inquiry. Public and general hearings were held, with the intention of designing measures which would promote and improve safety in this industry. I believe the hon. member for Vegreville said that about 6,000 pages of testimony were recorded at that time.
The initial report of the railway safety inquiry came out in April, 1972. This recorded the proceedings and hearings to do with causes and circumstances connected with specific accidents, and indicated that a dangerous commodities task force, an advisory committee on railway safety, and a new CTC accident investigation team would be established.
The third report came out in December, 1973, and contained the committee's findings and recommendations affecting specific areas such as signal systems, staff training, slide detector fences and other matters. This report indicated that the earlier formed railway safety advisory committee which consisted, as hon. members know, of representatives from CNR, CPR, commission experts and others, would work immediately on the conclusions and findings of the general inquiry, and provide a forum for discussions on matters affecting railway safety. The work of the advisory committee is on a continuing basis. As I say, if it is not doing the job I am the first to agree that pressure should be continually applied to ensure that indeed it does the job.
Between 20 and 25 per cent of all railway accidents occur at level crossings. I am sure that all hon. members can think back to not long ago when someone was killed at a level crossing. There again we are continually helping in the construction of signals and other protective devices for the safety and convenience of the public at level crossings.

October 28, 1974
Railway Safety
However, as long as there are human beings we will encounter a certain number of accidents.
I do not know how low you can cut these accidents, but I can assure hon.members that the government and MOT will continue to strive to reduce the level, and to improve the safety and standards of our railroads. It will take a good deal of money to renew, rebuild and expand the rail network to accommodate the larger, heavier type of equipment that will be required in the next 10 or 15 years, but it must be done with an eye to the safety of people, both those operating the railroads and the general public. As I said, human error will always be with us.
I support the intent and principle of the motion, except that I believe we now have the necessary procedures. We have only to ensure they are working. I do not feel a royal commission would in any way help to resolve the problems outlined so well by the hon. member for Rimouski.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, as this is my first occasion to speak in this House, may I personally extend my congratulations to you on your appointment.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ROYAL COMMISSION STUDY TO IMPROVE SAFETY OF PASSENGERS AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ROYAL COMMISSION STUDY TO IMPROVE SAFETY OF PASSENGERS AND EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
I, too, wish to applaud the comments of the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard). However, I cannot in honesty support his desire or claim for a royal commission.
The hon. member's motion suggests that a royal commission could eliminate accidents, including derailments of freight and passenger trains. Despite its value I do not think any royal commission could stop a train, at a given position at a given time, if some crazy fool driver, such as a number we have in this country today, crosses a right of way.
I grew up in the west. At the age of three I travelled with my father from Vancouver to Calgary and back. I can recall the old steamers going through the various canyons of the Rockies. In those days our safety features left much to be desired. In that period we had some terrible times. Perhaps senior members of the House will recall some of the accidents that occurred, particularly in the Fraser Canyon.
In the past few years we have seen some remarkable changes take place in the Fraser Canyon. Many of the hazards that existed on both railroads have been practically eliminated. I agree they cannot all be eliminated in one or two years. I am sure hon. members who have spoken will agree with that.
We have a railway safety advisory committee which has been operative for a number of years. Hon. members know the people who are on this committee. But I do not know whether hon. members are aware of what this committee has been doing for the past few years. There are many places in British Columbia where the in-depth study, begun in 1970, has now become a reality, particularly in some of the more remote areas.
I do not know whether hon. members are aware that this committee has already looked into the design, installation, inspection and maintenance of railway signal systems. Many years ago this was undertaken "by guess and by

golly" in some parts of the canyons and the Rockies. When the block system came in, it meant something.
We have now reached the electronic age. Because of the unit trains that have been brought in there is a desire for a more complete system of safety measures. This is what I am getting at in my comments.
The committee has studied the training of signal staff. Here we come to the human element. All too often this is the real cause of railroad accidents. We must not overlook this human factor, as it will always be with us.
I wish to deal with one area that was overlooked for many years, the hotbox and dragging equipment detectors. I do not know how many members watched trains go by at night with half a dozen hotboxes flaring like mad. No one seemed to bother. Today they have been eliminated. The railway safety committee has been doing its job.
The committee is also studying the identification and interpretation of signals by engine crews. There was a time when the crews had to work for hours and hours. The safety factor was not considered. The engineer and his fireman had to put in "X" number of hours before being relieved. I recall occasions in the early twenties when some of those men worked 23 or 24 hours without being relieved. Is it any wonder that accidents occurred?
Next I want to deal with the installation, operation and maintenance of slide detector fences. This is one of the finest jobs being done by our railroads. This work is being carried out in parts of my constituency by the B.C. railroad, CNR and CPR. It is being done to eliminate the dangers. We had one serious accident last winter. An inquiry was made into the matter, with the outcome that the situation has since been remedied. This came out of the railway safety committee.
I can understand the concern of the hon. member for Rimouski about these problems which exist in his part of the country, as they do also in mine. However, with the railway safety committee which we have, we do not need a royal commission. That would probably foul up everything. It would take over some of the work that is already in progress. In this case it is work which has been carried on for a number of years.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, just before five o'clock Your Honour called attention to the procedure to be followed on second reading and pointed out that our rules do not allow for detailed discussion of a bill clause by clause. My own remarks related to a general amendment which I hope will be incorporated in the bill. I merely indicated the clause at which it might be inserted. I had no intention of going through the bill clause by clause, because I knew it would be out of order to do so.
Just before the break for private members' hour I was about to quote from a public notice issued this year by the Federal Communications Commission in Washington, as follows:
Whether effective or not, such broadcasts are clearly intended to be deceptive.
This House, Mr. Speaker, acting on behalf of the citizens of Canada, does not need to be convinced that these subliminal advertising techniques are effective. We have only to be convinced that they are intended to be deceptive in order to effect an amendment to Bill C-2. The Parliament of Britain took this decision ten years ago, in 1964, and I feel it is time for Canada to do the same in the interests of consumers.
Whether this is the appropriate bill in which to make this change in our law is open to question. However, I feel the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), as the minister responsible for the interests of all consumers in Canada, should be responsible for enforcing this regulation rather than the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier). As an alternative procedure I considered an amendment to a private member's bill sponsored by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) dealing specifically with children's advertising. The bill has been before the House already, on another occasion.
Criticism of my proposal has come from the advertising and broadcasting industries, suggesting that I propose to outlaw a myth. I respectfully suggest that the contention advanced by those who call the use of subliminal techniques "a myth" has been exploded. I have evidence that this technique has been used in Canada. I also have an assurance from the Canadian Advertising Advisory Board that it has no objection to parliament banning the use of this technique. In fact, it was the board which recommended to me that the easiest way in which to do this would be through an amendment to Bill C-2, now before us. I know the House has other pressing matters before it,
Combines Investigation Act
but I trust hon. members will take time in which to review this proposal.
Since my endeavour to ban subliminal advertising became public a few months ago I have received letters and phone calls from consumers across Canada endorsing my position. The Canadian Civil Liberties Association and the Council of Women of Ottawa and Area are two groups I should like to mention in this regard.
As of August 21, 1974, the Canadian Association of Broadcasters has banned the use of subliminal techniques in children's advertising. No similar ban on commercials directed to adults has yet been effected by CAB. I would point out that a ban on the use of such techniques in all advertising was imposed by the National Association of Broadcasters in the United States in 1958. However, in 1974 this self-regulatory code was still being abused. I quote from public notice No.08055 dated January 24, 1974, issued by the Federal Communications Commission in Washington regarding the offending advertisement I cited earlier:
Despite the Code Authority's action, some stations apparently continued to broadcast spots containing the "Get it" statement.
Surely the House should follow the much more effective example of the United Kingdom, rather than follow an approach by self-regulation which clearly does not work.
Parliament should put the responsibility for misleading and deceptive advertising where it truly belongs, that is to say, with the manufacturers of products who become clients of advertising agencies.
I have a letter from the advertising agency which produced the children's toy advertisement I cited earlier. The agency stated:
We seriously questioned the advisability of using the subliminal "Get it" and so informed the client. The client, however, insisted that it be put in. Under such circumstances ... we had no choice but to put it in.
This may not be an isolated situation. However, it is the only one which has been discovered. It was not discovered by the self-regulatory body, C.A.A.B.; it was discovered by Robert Choate in Washington who brought it to the attention of the FCC there. In Canada action was taken to amend the children's code of ethics nine months after the advertisement was used.
I respectfully submit that Bill C-2 is the legislative instrument which could be used to rid Canada of this dangerous and deceptive practice. I hope all members, especially those on the other side of the House who are apparently in agreement with what I have been saying, will support Bill C-2 on second reading so that it can be referred, at an early date, to the committee where these matters can be dealt with fully.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the fact that consumers need a more adequate voice has had the support of this parliament since 1967, and it has had the support of all balanced people I have met in the business community no matter in what scale of endeavour they are involved. The bill we are considering is "to overcome the bad effects of concentration and misleading advertising in

October 28, 1974
Combines Investigation Act
the market place". That is a very well thought out and worded concept, and I agree with its thrust.
The purpose of the Combines Investigation Act, and again I quote "is to assist in maintaining effective competition as a prime stimulus to the achievement of maximum production, distribution and employment in a mixed system of public and private enterprise". Again this wording is concise, and I must compliment the work of the former minister of consumer and corporate affairs who served the twenty-ninth parliament. However, I seriously question the ability of this measure in its present form, unfinished, I must suggest, to achieve these desired goals.
I would seriously question the sincerity of the government in its repeated attempts to serve the consumer. Since October, 1967, this country has had four ministers and seven years' work leading up to the legislation we are debating now. I would ask the indulgence of the House to allow me to go back to Hansard of October 13,1967, in order to put a few things in perspective. Let me quote from what was said by the minister then in charge of the Department of the Registrar General. He said at that time, as reported at page 3068 of Hansard:
I believe, sir, that a significant step was taken earlier, when the Department of the Registrar General was established in 1966, at which time we brought together for the first time a number of functions relating to corporations, combines, patents, trade marks and bankruptcies, in order to ensure the better coordination of policy in these fields.
I would ask hon. members to remember the word coordination, which was part of the concept and concern of the minister at that time. I go on to quote the minister from the same page:
The consumer's association of Canada appealed to the government as early as 1960 and on numerous later occasions to create a department which would be responsible for the interests of consumers.
It is now 14 years since that initial request was made as stated that day. Let me refer again to the same speech where the minister stated:
The opinion that consumers need a more adequate voice in government has received parliamentary support.
That was said on October 13, 1967, and I believe that idea has had parliamentary support since. Let me continue to quote from the debate of that day, at page 3107 as follows: The present Department of the Registrar General and the agencies now grouped within it will be continued under a department with a new name, the department of corporate and consumer affairs, to which will be added two further responsibilities; first, the responsibility to coordinate programs for consumer affairs at the federal level, initiate new programs, and so on; second, the responsibility for representing the federal government in the area of corporate securities.
Let me now quote an interesting sidelight to the debate of that date. This was the same minister speaking, and he was referring to the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Neilsen) and the present hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). He said:
I should like to say to the hon. member for Yukon and the hon. member for Bow River in particular, in answer to some of their suggestions, that this department will not be a bureaucratic monster. On one occasion I said that if you want to use the vocabulary of the octopus of government, this is not a new tentacle; it is a rearrangement of the existing tentacles, and no more.
Again during that debate, and for the second time in the same day, he referred to the responsibility for coordination of acts under this department by stating:

I should like to say also that this department will not involve more government spending. When I spoke on my estimates I said that this year the department would have an expenditure of $8 million, less $6 million by way of revenue in respect of patent applications, bankruptcies, incorporation applications, and so on; so, the cost to the Canadian taxpayer will be between $1.5 million and $2 million. There will be not additional cost of any significance because, as I said, aside from the hiring of certain specialists in the area of consumer affairs most of the staff is available in the various agencies of the federal government.
The minister at that time was extremely concerned as evidenced by those comments, but what has happened since 1967? We must look at the growth of this embryo reorganization or this rearrangement of the tentacles. The corporate and consumer affairs of 1967-68 involved a vote of $11,338,000. The consumer affairs' portion was $4 million. In the recent estimates for 1974-75 that $11 million has grown to more than $43,755,000, and the consumers' part involves over $17.5 million. I would ask you to remember the original estimate of the cost in 1967, namely $1.5 million to $2 million. I suggest the tentacle rearrangement has grown into an octopus.
The anti-business feeling in this country grows in almost direct proportion to the increase in government spending. If this rate of growth keeps up the bankruptcy branch of this department is going to be very busy.
This legislation has been debated for over seven years, and is now being presented to us in an unfinished state. We are now being asked by the minister to let a committee finish it. Why we are being asked to do that? As a backbencher my resources and time do not allow me to participate fully in this committee, yet my constituents and the people of that area of this country from which I come demand that I show an interest in this type of legislation.
The minister has a budget of $43,755,000. Has the government become tired and does it now admit it cannot do the job? Can it not give us a tidy presentation, properly researched, in order that we can vote on it in principle on second reading? Why are the amendments being kept in the wings? Why have they not been tabled for the consideration of members in caucus? I would ask why is there all this mystery?
We have seen rule by regulation, then rule by ministerial discretion, and now we are seeing rule by commission. This has all taken place since 1967, and I suggest it has left the business sector of Canada with a confused decision making base. I do not think that the problems we see today in Italy, Britain, Japan and in the United States will be easily solved, but one of our first steps must be an attack against this confusion of decision making based here in Canada.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) referred to our balance of payments. Let me remind the minister that 55 per cent of commercial activity in this country involves small business, and small businesses do not have the resources to handle the confusion and legislative load that are resulting from the change in the tax act.
Surely clean, tidy legislation under the control of parliament is the least the minister should offer the country and parliament at this time. Regulatory fever is rampant in this government. Business is starting to operate defensively. I mentioned the trouble other trading nations with
October 28, 1974

which we deal are facing. Trivia and regulations are snuffing out the light and fire of Canadian business. The standard of living of the Canadian people is very dependent on a vital, aggressive business community.
The previous speaker mentioned the scale of business, and the fact that if people in the Canadian work force wish to have a decent standard of living they would have to work for large companies. That may be so, but a large portion of the community is the small business segment. It is this segment which suffers as a result of such self-imposed legislation.
It is a sad fact of life that people who abuse their freedom in the performance of business functions, through overzealous acts of self-interest, are the cause of this type of legislation. If these people had compassion for those who work with them, under them, and around them, there would not be a need for this type of legislation.
I have not noted in respect of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs any expenditure of talent or effort directed toward the business community, the present managers and new managers, so that they would have an awareness of the importance of their function and the importance of serving the people, the employees, the customers, the suppliers, the community and the country. Nowhere in Bill C-2, or in the work of the department, do I find any indication of effort in this direction. If there had been a move in this direction in 1968 I doubt very much if there would be need for such a bill being debated in this House today. Where is the corporate part of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in this area of educational need? I ask the minister to give this consideration because here is an area that is waiting to be serviced.
I should now like to turn to the aspect of the bill in respect of misleading statements and advertising. The minister in this bill, and in statements to the media, offers strict rules of conduct for private enterprise. He has threatened these sinister people with jail and fines. I agree. But why does the minister apply these rules of his just society-if I may use that term-to only one minority group? What process of logic causes the minister to exclude other aspects of our community from his sanctions? What about political parties and politicians who use misleading statements or misleading advertising, or who are guilty of not having kept promises? Frankly, I would mention stuffed ballot boxes at both ends of the country. Why are there not fines and jail sentences for this group which lacks credibility in statements to the public?

Surely this is misleading advertising.
The 1972-1973 report of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs on page 11 exaggerates by 100,000 the caseload involved. Is this misleading or is it an honest

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in the debate on this bill which has been called the competition bill, but which in effect does not deal with the problems of competition which are outside its scope. Nevertheless, I think this is a good opportunity to take part in a debate on the effects of competition on our economy and national life.
I agree with the aim of the bill, but it seems to me that there is serious doubt as to whether it will accomplish what it sets out to do. Also, I believe that perhaps its basic tenets should be questioned. We should ascertain at what level competition should exist, and in what manner.
We have entered into an era of consumer concern and consumer interest because of the modern philosophy that anyone who performs a service or manufactures an article is essentially considered to perform a poor service, or to do poor workmanship, unless the government is there to oversee it. The consumer, on the other hand, according to the current mode of thinking, must always have perfect service and perfect articles. We recognize that there are people in our society who think that the service that they receive is always poor, and the articles they purchase always defective. We recognize that such people are present in our society, and to provide a system of competition tailored to their needs would be almost impossible.
This attitude has been made worse by our present method of job creation. Many people are not producers either in the manufacturing or in the service areas, and often they have little concept of what is involved in providing a service or manufacturing an article. Similarly, as a result of automation the narrow scope of many jobs gives little opportunity to an individual to understand the complexity of many services, and the complexity of the manufacture of many products.
I believe that the attitude that service should be always perfect and manufactured articles flawless has been aggravated by the great difficulty of getting top rate people to fill executive positions. A classic example can be found in our hospitals where it is increasingly difficult to find well trained people to accept the top positions. There are many people in the lower categories of employment in hospitals who could take on more complicated executive posts, and yet they are content to work at lower levels because their take home pay is almost the same and they do not have to shoulder the heavier responsibilities.
I make these observations because I think they have a fundamental bearing on competition within our economy.

The rise of consumerism is very real, and much greater attention is being paid to it than in the past. At the same time consumers have been demanding a higher and higher level of service and quality of goods. Also at the same time many factors in our economy work against the provision of a high level of service. Some people would suggest that this is due to the profit motive, but I suggest that many other factors are working against providing the high level of service required in our society.
What about the aim of the bill before us, and what are some of the things it may do? So far as industrial strategy is concerned, this legislation grew out of the interim report on competition policy issued by the Economic Council of Canada in 1969. That was five years ago. No studies have been undertaken by the government, or by any other agency, on what the consequences have been since that time of a strict regulation of domestic competition on Canada's competitive position in the world markets. Since I came here six years ago it has always been the view of the government that we should have a Canadian industrial strategy, but it has never been clear what this should be, Mr. Speaker. Invariably it was considered to mean a reduction in the export of raw materials and an increase in the export of manufactured goods.
It has been known for a long time that in our foreign trade we have had a deficit in manufactured goods, and there are no signs of improvement. In 1972 we had a deficit of $1,505 million in fabricated and end products. In 1973 the deficit was $2,207 million, and in 1974 it could well go to $4 billion. If it were not for the strong position of our raw materials surplus we would be very badly off insofar as foreign trade is concerned.
This bill could have a profound effect on the industrial economy of the country. For instance, one of the great earners of foreign exchange for Canada has been prairie grain. In the six years that I have been here the government has made the productivity of that part of the country more difficult to achieve. Indeed, after the settlement of the west coast grain strike which has contributed to inflation, and the settlement of the maritime strike on the great lakes, farmers have been discouraged from producing more grain. This is partly due to the government's past actions in not ensuring the smooth flow of grain and in allowing a stoppage in grain handling by a small group of people.
This bill does not do anything about Crown corporations, or about the three levels of government that are often responsible for preventing competition. It is those three levels of government that have often been the culprits in preventing competition and, as a result, preventing services from being provided. I will outline how the government of Canada and its offshoot, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and the Manitoba government and its offshoot, the Manitoba telephone system, have prevented my riding from receiving a second television channel, and this in the name of good government, although in reality it was interference in the broadcasting business.
For the number of years most of the riding that I represent has had only one TV channel from Yorkton,
