Saskatchewan, which was classified as a CBC Affiliate. Numerous efforts were made to try to get a second network, CTV, into the area. After long and extensive hearings, finally the CRTC approved the application of Mof-fatt Communications Ltd., to provide service for a second channel.
In the meantime CBC had bought the antenna situated on Baldy Mountain in the Duck Mountain Provincial Park. That was sold to it by the private station in Yorkton, the Skinner interest. The Baldy Mountain tower is the only spot that will cover the area with a proper TV signal. Moffatt Communications applied for permission to situate their tower on this Baldy Mountain spot, but were refused permission by the Manitoba government.
In negotiations the Canadian Broadcasting Company has demanded $15,000 to strengthen the present tower for the CTV antenna, plus $10,000 a year for rental. Privately, this could be made available through another broadcasting company for $10,000, and rental of $5,000 per year, just half of what the CBC is charging, but they are prevented from using this by the actions of the Manitoba government.
Now the federal government enters into it. Another park comes between the tower and the Brandon station. It is Riding Mountain National Park which is run very poorly. It would have been necessary to instal a microwave tower but this was vetoed by the federal government on the grounds that it would detract from the wilderness aspect of the park.
As well, the Manitoba government and Communications Canada have almost made it a policy that there will be no private microwave communications set up, at least in the province of Manitoba. The alternate way to carry the signal is through the Manitoba Telephone System but, here again, the prices quoted for carrying the signal have been high, and considered by the private company to be exorbitant. That is why Moffatt Communications have wanted to have their own private microwave system. Whether or not the Manitoba Telephone System, which is very much the arm of the Manitoba government, has made a fair quotation, I do not know. But the fact is that the Manitoba Telephone System is in a monopoly position, and there in not even an independent board to examine whether or not its quotation is reasonable.
I cannot see that this bill will be useful in preventing this kind of extortion. The federal government, the provincial government, the CBC which is a Crown corporation, and the Manitoba Telephone System are combining to prevent a second television channel. Will this bill prevent such a thing? The answer seems to be absolutely not. In this case it is not the huge private corporations that are preventing competition; it is our own two governments, our own public corporations.
I should now like to turn to the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission, which is an integral part of this bill. The aim of this commission will be to judge whether or not certain business practices are within the realm of fair competition or are restrictive. The government contends that it will be in the interests of small business. The commission itself is seemingly going to interpret the situations that come before it on a legal basis rather than a commercial basis.
Combines Investigation Act
Now, Mr. Speaker, what may seem like a legal discriminatory practice in the commercial world becomes not so clear in the legal world. Many small businesses are able to carry on because they have exclusive agencies in their area. But, if a supplier must sell to all people merchandising in that area, such as small chain stores, the small businessman is soon put at a disadvantage. Much merchandise in our society is not sold on a strictly price basis. Most small retail establishments are viable, not because they sell cheaper than large chain stores but because of the personality of their owner, or their manager, or their clerks, and because they have certain exclusive lines.
To do away completely with exclusive selling rights, at least in retailing, would probably do much more harm than good. I can give you an example that actually happened in my area. An individual retailing a certain brand of paint found that his competitor, a fairly large retail store, was able to retail the paint at less than his actual wholesale cost. He had no alternative but to cease carrying on his business.
There are many examples of where a small business would be put at a very decided disadvantage if this clause were completely carried out. There is no doubt that, on a strictly price basis, large chain stores have enormous advantages inherent in their structure over the small private business.
Then again I notice that when there are violations of various government regulations by business, it is invariably the small businessman who gets penalized. He has not the expertise or the legal help available that large corporations have. Furthermore, a conviction against him is much more damaging to him as his clientele know him, than it is to a countrywide retailing organization.
Government commissions that are expected to show some results for their efforts, have a tendency to clobber the easiest available victim. After all, most of these commissions have to show some evidence of earning their keep, and the small individual is the easiest to intimidate.
Again, many of the government's tests for a basis of measurement, are open to serious question. One I have heard of is that meat inspectors take only one gram of meat to test for fatty content. Mr. Speaker, this is far too small a sampling to arrive at any real assessment of the fat and lean content of the meat.
I think everyone is in favour of increasing competition, but the methods whereby we assess and lay down the guidelines are extremely important not just to competition but to the whole pattern of industrial life in this country. Under this bill the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission seems to be adopting a decidedly legal viewpoint. But the legal view of what industry and commerce should be doing as regards competition is vastly different from the practical aspects of business. The effect of this commission can be nationwide, and can shape the commercial activity of the country for decades to come.
Contrary to the stated aim the commission will be biased against the small individual businessman as opposed to the large corporations, and since the whole thrust of government is overwhelmingly against small business it makes one wonder if, for all its good intentions, the net effect will be a further curtailment and harass-

ment of small business life. I hope that in committee we will get a few more of the answers, Mr. Speaker. I think it is unfortunate that the bill, which had extensive hearings in committee last time, was not reintroduced with the amendments that the minister has stated will be brought forward.

This bill, the content of which is similar to that of bill C-227 tabled in the House on November 5, 1973, and to that of bill C-7 which was tabled on February 28, 1974 and died on the order paper because of the general election has had no luck at all, Mr. Speaker.
I think the opposition has kept very well in mind the recommendations of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs in June 1971, while he insisted upon the fact this bill aimed, and I quote: to promote discussion rather than enforcement-
For once the Minister was listened to. However, after having heard many opposition speakers, I am afraid that such discussion may drag on probably because of a lack of precision from the Minister regarding the proposed amendments.
I understand that the minister wants to put more bite into the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission which has certainly failed to do the job expected from it, but at the same time extremes must be avoided.
The first purpose of this bill is to specify certain prohibitions dealing with trade practices which are detrimental to the Canadian consumers, prohibitions creating offences, and to bring in desirable amendments to existing prohibitions.
On reading this bill clause by clause, we find that it deals with everything to give more scope to the definitions and to give the investigators more work to do; there will be more of them, and thus more summonses and steeper fines.
I sometimes wonder whether that will protect the small businessmen, including farmers, while offering the consumer one last hope. I doubt it, Mr. Speaker, for it is proved by experience that the big multi-national companies like the huge cartels, in production as well as in marketing, will always find a way to pay the accountants, economists and lawyers needed to evade the law or to avail themselves of some protection of which the people will be unaware.
In his statement, the minister listed the topics dealt with in the bill such as, for instance, advertising. He wants to be stricter and suggests that the committee 
should also be more severe with regard to advertising. Mr. Speaker, I agree with him on that point, and wonder why the bill was not introduced before the election: it would certainly have created a furore during the campaign.
As for "misleading advertising", I do not have to give many examples. A little while ago, we talked about bad advertising for children. I think that the Crown Corporation and private networks, like all news media, should come under the provisions of this legislation and cease misleading the Canadian people. I am confident that the members of the committee will be patient enough to listen and to implement the advice of those who will appear before them.
Then, the hon. Minister, speaking about "dual pricing", said and I quote:
Then any sale at a price other than the lower of two or several prices is prohibited in the case of double ticketed product.
In my opinion, if we dug deeper, we could get to the famous legislation on fraudulent bankruptcies. I have noticed it several times, because I have been in business for forty years and I know that the company or the fellow who goes bankrupt fraudulently comes out much richer than before.
After having establish two companies, a purchase company and a "resale" company, thus being able to sell at a price lower than the billing, causing prejudice to all other dealers and even threatening to make some honest dealers go bankrupt, the bankrupt will not be prepared, after a couple of weeks, to start a new business. That is sheer honesty. A section of the fraudulent bankruptcies legislation deals with that situation.
As far as "pyramid selling" is concerned, we agree that legislation should be more rigid. You can be assured of our support on this.
A little further, the bill deals with the "refusal to sell". On that matter, we must be very careful. If this bill were implemented, the farmer would be in serious trouble, because he sells to small dealers at $2.50 a bag potatoes which he sold for $2 to the big supplier. The committee will certainly have representations to make on this matter.
I think "gift selling" could be added to "tied selling". That is the big scheme today. Big companies try to sell second-quality goods by offering a gift of little value. The customer is mainly attracted by the gift, and she will buy the merchandise to get it. In my opinion, this clause of the bill will provide some protection to the consumer.
In our regions, and I assume that the same goes for all others, there is a "market restriction", that is territorial limitation in order to avoid competition from outside. I think that if this bill is accepted, it will outwit many companies that want to control each and every territory and maintain prices in all sectors.
As for proceedings for damages and losses resulting from conduct contrary to the legislation I wonder-I keep asking myself the same question-whether it is fair for

the small businessman, distributor or producer who will be affected by this clause. I should like the clause to be broad enough to cover the big tradesmen.
Mr. Speaker, we are in favour of submitting the private enterprise to a healthy competition, since it was honest competition that normalized consumer prices in the past. To achieve this, we need laws. I say once again here tonight that lack of competition is as detrimental in production as it is in marketing.
Today we live in an era of large mergers, national and international cartels, absolute controls over marketing and, we must admit, over production.
Producers, I would say thousands of them, paid with the life of their business for the elimination of this competition under the false pretext of profitability.
If the government is really serious, it will have to come to grips with the most dictatorial of all since it is the cause of stagnation. Because of that, the legislation we pretend to improve today achieve nothing. I am referring to the monopoly of banks. I think that is the first that eliminated any competition among banks. It will be the first to reestablish order so that we finally control the discounts of the Bank of Canada and the freeze, if necessary.
Only with those basic controls shall he begin to work in the interest of consumers so that they no longer pay two, three or even five times the price of goods and services necessary for their survival.
I hope that the bill will be sent to the Standing Committee to give the public a chance to be heard, especially by the government.
The government was accused of not having detailed its amendments enough. Members of the committee should seize the opportunity to introduce amendments and invite regional bodies to appear before the committee.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take this opportunity to congratulate the minister on his new portfolio. I wish him well in what is going to be a very difficult and, I am sure, exciting area of work.
I am sure all members of parliament, certainly those on this side, agree that the elements of this bill which have to do with consumer legislation need to be passed, and passed rapidly. I do not think anyone opposes legislation to restrict pyramid selling, subliminal advertising, misleading advertising and so forth. Such actions should have been prohibited long ago. The sooner they are dealt with, the better off we will be.
The fundamental thrust of this bill, especially certain parts of the legislation, are of great significance. In fact, I feel this legislation is as important to the ongoing economic development of the country as the budget which will be presented quite soon.
Not surprisingly we have had legislation to deal with competition for a long time. In fact we have had anti-combines legislation for almost 100 years, the first being intro-
Combines Investigation Act
duced by the Conservative party, and so it is not unusual that we would support this type of bill. But we want it to be a bill responsive to the fundamental needs of the notion.
In the British tradition as a nation we have taken the position that the way in which the consumer is best protected is by the operation of truly competitive markets. Anyone who has followed the development of classical economic policy knows very well that it is difficult to dispute the fact that when you have competitive markets you have the optimum allocation of resources, and the greatest production possible in the economy. Indeed, for many years it also was argued that a competitive economy automatically assured levels of full employment.
In addition, and again in the British tradition, it was believed that with many small firms operating there was the maximum amount of political freedom. It is not a matter of accident that the great British libertarians such as Acton and John Stuart Mill believed in competitive markets.
Many of the arguments advanced for competition bills and competition legislation have not been economic. And it is not a coincidence that countries such as Germany and others on the European continent, which have never been interested in maintaining competitive markets, have had great difficulty in developing democratic processes such as we have in this country.
Underlying this legislation is therefore not only the whole question of effective markets but also the question of the concentration of power and, indeed, associated with that, the question of true economic freedom.
There was no challenge to the proposition that there was need for strong competition legislation until the 1930's when Lord Keynes introduced his general theory, which demonstrated that there was no automated guarantee that competitive markets alone assured full employment. As a consequence of the depression, emphasis on the goals of full employment and price stability have become so great that interest in competition legislation has dropped to a very considerable extent.
In fact since 1946 we have neglected competition policy to a very dangerous degree. Indeed, the adoption of a Keynesian philosophy, that we could get full employment and price stability by broad macro-economic policies led many to believe that competition policy really did not matter. Since 1946 we in this country have had no effective anti-competition policy at all.
Perhaps it was only by chance that the rise in interest in monetary and fiscal policy as the tools for attaining full employment and price stability came along at exactly the same time as great changes in technology, a large increase in transport facilities, great increases in communication systems, the possibility of serving larger markets, economies of scale, the development of multi-national firms, the development of agro-business and the change from the isolated local union to the great national unions, but the results of these changes also led to a decline in interest in competition policy.
In fact over the last 30 years the power and size of certain sectors of our economy have become so large it is really a fundamental question of whether traditional anti-

October 28, 1974
Combines Investigation Act
combines policy makes any sense. I am sure everyone knows that some economists, particularly Professor Galbraith of Harvard, have taken the position that anti-combines policy is ineffective in many areas and that it is a waste of time to try and put it into effect. It is argued by such people that certain sectors of our society are so large they are not responsive to what is happening in the economy, but make the economy operate for their benefit. If this is true-and markets are not competitive and cannot be made competitive-will traditional economic policies designed to bring about price and employment stability, work?
Why is it, one has to ask, we have not been able to achieve full employment and price stability at the same time in recent years? Why is it that broad policies do not work in the way they are expected to work? Is it because of the structure of our markets? If so, is there any chance that anti-combines policy will be able to assure a structure that will permit broad policies to work more effectively? Perhaps more important, have we reached a stage at which we may have lost many individual freedoms which are associated with the competitive market structure? Again, it has been argued strongly that large concentrations of power do not really make much difference because they countervail each other. This is the Galbraith thesis-there is no point in trying to break up large economic units because they constitute an effective brake against each other. However, in an article by Richard Goodwin recently on the dilemma of the United States economy, the point was made that these forces are apparently no longer countervailing. It does not make sense in this day and age, according to this author, to argue that large business conglomerations are countervailed by large unions and big government when, in fact, they all work together.
All of us hear the argument advanced that things are happening to society and to people that nobody wants to happen, even those who bring these things about, because the economy and the bureaucracy are so large and complex.
Therefore, in assessing competition legislation we have to consider these things: first, has the structure of our economy changed so much as a result of the economics of scale that the economic policies we put into effect in order to cope with inflation or bring about full employment simply will not now work? The evidence indicates that this may be the case. The question then arises: why don't they? The answer may be that these measures cannot work because there are concentrations of economic and political power. If this is so, we must seek, when looking at this legislation, to try to reverse the tendencies which are now in effect, or at least to examine the implications of these changes.
In the second place, can we in fact maintain individual freedom and liberty amid such concentrations of power? If not, how do we deal with competitive market structures? Where this legislation is terribly lacking is that it does not recognize all large power segments in our society. The question to be considered is not the simplistic question of whether or not we need more competition. That is not the serious issue. The serious issue is whether or not, after two decades of no really effective anti-trust laws, does it make

any sense to talk about this sort of legislation at all, and, if not, what are the alternative ways of protecting the consumer?
We know that what we are getting in terms of economic performance is very strange. We are astonished when interest rates rise and inflation does not slow down. The reason must be that the structure of the economy is changing dramatically, and the old techniques are no longer working.
In another sense, what does this legislation mean in terms of the retention of freedom in the economy as a whole? The essence of the competitive system is to bring a high degree of individual freedom, initiative and opportunity into economic performance. If we allow the concentration of power which has gone on for so long to continue, shall we be able to retain those freedoms which are so important to us?
Associated with all this is the fact that we are moving away from the dominance of the rule of law to the rule of men. In this legislation, just as in the Foreign Investment Review Act, a tribunal is being appointed with no clear or definite indication of what the tribunal is to do. Democracy cannot survive when the rule of men replaces the rule of law.
We have taken away from parliament in the past few years the function of being the trustee of the people's money. It is impossible for members of parliament to review the estimates in any effective fashion. It may be that sheer growth has done this. However, this does not remove from us the responsibility for looking carefully at the serious issues which are before the country and I suggest to the minister that the manner in which the legislation has been considered up to this stage makes it important that we go back to the committee, call witnesses and examine the fundamental issues involved. Today we are not really in a parliament which is the same as that of the last few years.
No observer of the economic forces which have been unleashed in the world today can be sanguine about the way in which the economic situation is developing. What will really destroy the system of democracy is a continued pretence that things have not changed. There is an unreadiness to face economic realities.
The reality of the Canadian economy is that we have developed large segments in which competition is not present. We have never acknowledged this in realistic fashion; we have always found reasons to exempt certain sections from the play of market forces. The net result is that policies which once worked, and which we hope will work, will not work any more.
Consequently I hope the minister who is responsible for this legislation will in fact agree that, when we go back to the committee, we should take a look at the legislation again in a broader sense, and that it be studied to see whether there are sectors in the economy that are fundamentally non-competitive that must be brought in to the bill, but which are not now in the bill simply because of the way our society and economy are organized. The problems for our economic system and our democratic government are indeed very serious.
October 28, 1974

The belief is growing on the part of more and more people in this country that governments are not able to deal with the problems which most people face. There is evidence to suggest that these people may be right. We have evidence over the last five years that would indicate that perhaps we cannot obtain relatively stable prices.
People are beginning to really believe that we cannot have stable prices. We have forgotten the proposition that people have the hope of owning their own homes, valued at about two and half times their annual income. Perhaps we do not believe that is possible any longer. We have forgotten the proposition that we can solve some of these national energy problems, and people are beginning to believe that governments cannot govern.
People are constantly being reinforced in the feeling that governments refuse to look at the reality of many issues. It seems to me that the real question is whether the government will have the courage and the conviction to look at the structure of the Canadian economy and assess whether the 19th century competition approach is valid, or whether the Canadian economy has changed to the degree that our learned contemporary fiscal and monetary policies will not now work. The government must decide whether our current policies will work or whether they are counterproductive.
Until these questions are answered, the bill in its present form is not ready to become law.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always a little hesitant when I follow the learned hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies), particularly on a subject covering an area that has been grey for quite sometime, but an area that we are now trying to bring into sharp contrast. I should, in any event, like to add my congratulations to those already expressed to the minister in his new portfolio. I wish him well.
As has been pointed out, there are a number of good points in this legislation such as those in respect of referral and pyramid selling. Sometimes I feel that those areas have been looked after under provincial legislation. I wonder sometimes if we are not duplicating already existing legislation for the purpose of putting window dressing on a bill that is very difficult to sell to the people.
My concerns this evening are not in that very wide and general concept covered by the hon. member for Don Valley. My concerns this evening are in respect of that segment of industry with which I am reasonably familiar, namely, the construction industry.
The construction industry lives and thrives on competition. All construction type projects are subject to competitive bid, so that competition is not entirely new to the construction industry. Yet in the past we have found that some contractors run afoul of the combines legislation. I suppose it is fair to ask why they run afoul of this law.
If anyone who has been involved with a construction industry asks himself why this could happen he will immediately realize that pricing is tough in this industry and, when things are difficult, you cut back, and cut back again. This is the general situation in this segment of industry. People often have difficulty meeting overheads, and on occasion some contractors get together in order to avoid bankruptcy. In this way prices gradually work back
Combines Investigation Act
up to the point where contractors can begin to survive again. It is in this way that these people can run afoul of combines legislation.
I see new dangers inherrent in this new legislation that I have not seen previously. There is a whole range of fees now being charged by realtors, engineers, architects and, while I normally do not have much sympathy for them, even lawyers. If these people happen to charge a fee which is exactly the same as the fee charged by a competitor I see the possibility of them running afoul of this legislation. Once again these people operate in an area that is generally considered to be covered by provincial legislation. 1 question the need of driving a tack with a sledgehammer, as we perhaps seem to be doing in this area.
We must also consider the small businessman who runs, for example, a little electric sub-contracting company, or perhaps a plumber, a forming company, or an erecting company, people who operate in that whole gambit of bits and pieces that make up the construction industry. I wonder how any of those individuals would feel one morning to wake up facing a lawsuit? Perhaps such an action would require a decision by the supreme court. When one considers the amount of cost involved he will immediately realize that such a thing could bankrupt the small businessman.
The lawsuit I have in mind is one that might arise from something the small businessman had been doing in the past, but because of the passage of this new legislation he could be in difficulty. I had in mind the situation that could arise if a supplier wanted to give a prime contractor a lower price than the price he would normally sell his product to the industry. Experience has shown us that combines legislation tends to go against the small contractor.
The bigger contractors usually have sufficient staff to keep them out of trouble. In most cases they have sufficient finances to keep them in business during a lengthy court action. Small contractors receive many questionnaires from people like Statistics Canada. They are often forced to hire accountants or auditors to look after that type of thing. They receive all kinds of requests from an ever-increasing bureaucracy, all of which makes it more difficult to stay in business. This situation tends to get even worse when the companies become a little bigger. Let me give you one example of what I have in mind.
We have cement being delivered in southern Ontario for exactly the same price from three or four different companies manufacturing in different parts of Ontario. It is transported by two or three different means, over small or large areas, with seemingly no real competitive aspect. Yet because these are particularly large companies they seem to get away with it. The price per barrel, as it was formerly, although it is now changed, was identical. In addition these cement companies try to- tell us they are being competitive but at the same time they will not let the customer come to their plants and pick up the product. If a purchaser should have the equipment and wish to pick up the product he is not allowed to do so. He must purchase the product on their terms, and those terms are always alike.

October 28, 1974
Combines Investigation Act
Then we have the matter of shopping centres. Often builders and developers are involved in these shopping centres. In respect of this legislation I see a real problem, and it seems to me that shopping centres could be completely outlawed. The essence of a shopping centre is to prohibit another class of merchandise of exactly the same nature being sold on the premises. As I understand this legislation, that would not be allowed. There would not appear to be any competitive edge to the shopping centre.
I do not really think shopping centres are the big bogey man people once thought they would become. In my town there are three shopping centres, and the downtown area is thriving. I think they have proven to be an incentive. In other places in Ontario, such as Peterborough, there are huge shopping centres which have not hurt the downtown shopping area. However, I believe this legislation would prohibit shopping centres from doing what traditionally they have done.
As I see it, one of the most critical points in respect of this legislation is that it is the small businessman who will be hit. There is protection enough for the large businessman. Recently I ran into a situation which is indicative of what I have in mind.
In my riding there is a sheetmetal fabricator who produces a product in galvanized metal, which could be sold anywhere in southern Ontario. This company is unionized and pays union rates, which are less in this area than in metropolitan areas. Because this is a fairly effective and efficient operation the products of this company could be sold in Toronto, but the unions in Toronto to date have kept this company from doing business in Toronto. I see nothing in this legislation that would be of assistance in this case.
The union in Toronto is strong enough that it has been able to dictate to the manufacturers that none of this product is to be allowed into the metropolitan Toronto area, simply because the union rates paid by that company are lower than those paid in Toronto. This is an example of discrimination which should not be allowed. I have been unable to find anything in this legislation which would help that company.
Many things are covered by this legislation. There is the matter of the service industries. There are other radical changes being proposed. This legislation has been around now for two or three parliaments, under the direction of a couple of different ministers. I do not believe it would be harmful if we proceeded reasonably slowly.
I know there is a desire to get this bill before the standing committee, and I hope that in committee the minister will be receptive to a number of amendments and changes that will be proposed by his colleagues, on both sides of this House, who have business experience. Also I hope the bill, when brought back from the committee, will be changed quite drastically from its present form.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in this debate on a bill which is complicated and which will have far-reaching effects. The minister has indicated it is his intention to bring forward amendments when the bill goes to the committee.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
That is an excellent idea. This bill means more and more government involvement in the daily affairs of the businessman, yet the minister has called for its rapid passage. It covers three major areas. First it covers the consumer aspects such as misleading advertising, undesirable trading practices and undesirable retail practices. It covers certain regulatory aspects with regard to the restrictive Trade Practices Commission. The balance of the bill, of course, has to do with amateur and professional sports, and amendments to the Bank Act.
With regard to the sections of the bill dealing with the consumer I do not believe there is any real argument by members of the House. I think all members, particularly those who have practised law, will welcome the legislation dealing specifically with referral selling, pyramid selling, switch selling, and double ticketing, to mention a few matters. I have always been one who believed in the old Latin phrase used in English law, caveat emptor-let the buyer beware. This has been a rule I have always followed. Perhaps I have followed it because a number of years ago, when I first started work and was earning $30 a month, a very shrewd encyclopedia salesman visited me and sold me a set of encyclopedia. Since I was earning only $30 per month it took me some considerable time to pay for the books. Therefore I soon learned that one must be aware of salesmen and slick traders.
But after practising law for some 20 years I realize that many intelligent people never had an experience similar to mine, and were therefore taken in on occasion by slick salesmen who were involved in referral selling, in my area particularly in the field of roofing and siding for houses. Having met some of these slick salesmen, I can see how people were taken in by them. I believe that people must be protected from this sort of thing.
Regarding the regulatory aspects of the bill, the minister has indicated that this legislation will be used to regulate the larger corporations. But it does not specify what is a large corporation or a small business. Surely the bill could be amended to set forth in detail the definition of a large corporation and a small corporation, either on the basis of assets or on the basis of the volume of business.
Small businesses are the backbone of our economy. They are our largest employers. Yet we find more and more small businesses closing their doors every day. What is the reason for that? Basically the reason is increased government regulation, increased government controls. I spoke to several small businessmen in my constituency recently, very successful businessmen who are now due for retirement, and who would like to sell their businesses to some younger persons. However, they find that there are no young people interested, despite the fact that these are exceptionally good businesses.
When you speak to young people about taking over a business, what do they say? They say: "We do not want to get involved. We have no problem with borrowing money; there are such government sources as IDB, and so on, but we do not want to be shackled by government regulations and rules". What will happen to these small businesses? The people to whom I have spoken, in two cases of which I know, have tried to sell for some three years. Now they
October 28, 1974

have reached the stage where it is their intention to gradually liquidate their stock, sell their property, and retire. This, to a relatively small community, means a loss of jobs, with the resultant loss to our economy.
Personally I have no respect for the practices of the larger corporations which, because of their size, are able to protect themselves from competition. But I do have respect for the small businessman who operates best in a competitive market.
I was interested in reading about the competition policy from the 1969 report of the Economic Council of Canada. I would like to quote from it. That report states in part:
The institution and maintenance of a competition policy such as presently exists in Canada may be taken to reflect a belief that over a greater part of the economy, competitive market forces are potentially capable of allocating resources better and more cheaply with a less cumbersome administrative overhead than any alternative arrangement, such as wholesale public ownership and control, detailed government regulation of enterprise, or self-regulation by large industrial units within a corporate state. The function of competition policy is not to bring about a textbook regime of "perfect" competition in all the various markets making up the system, but rather to encourage the liberation of the system's maximum competitive potential, imperfect though this may be.
The resulting competition is valued not for itself, but for what it can accomplish, in putting resources to work efficiently and effectively. Thus, the market does the job and the government's main responsibility, so far as efficiency in resource allocation is concerned, is to see that the market is free to do the best job of which it is capable. Competition is relied upon as the prime mechanism of social control... ; competition itself should not be the objective, but rather the most important single means by which efficiency is achieved.
We must not lose sight of the principles set forth in that statement. I believe that to rush through this bill on the understanding that it will be amended in committee is wrong. It seems to me that the bill should be withdrawn now and additional amendments brought in, so that the bill will fall within the principles outlined in the report of the Economic Council.

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DEFINITIONS, POWERS OF INVESTIGATORS, OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with much attention and interest to the remarks from many hon. members. I must say that their comments will surely help me to improve this bill along with the members of the parliamentary committee that will examine this bill, to improve this extremely important legislation which many Canadians have been expecting for such a long time.
I believe that in closing this debate, it is important for me to ensure the hon. members of my intention to move amendments to the legislation, amendments which are for the most part the result of briefs and requests presented by Canadian agencies when this bill was studied by the last Parliament.
Combines Investigation Act
I should like nevertheless to point out certain remarks made during the second reading debate and especially a question put by the hon. member for York Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), namely whether that legislation was really an improvement on the present one. I do not believe this House would question the real desire for progress, the unshaken wish to serve people in a better way, on the part of the government as well as of the Economic Council of Canada, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, the Combines Investigation Branch and the numerous experts who were consulted throughout the very difficult revision of our competition policy, which in fact began in 1966.
That the results are on a level with the efforts, I believe, Mr. Chairman, that it will be generally agreed, as it was besides by a good number of members on both sides of the House, who spoke during this debate. They recognized the merits as well as the urgency of such a legislation.
But can one really refuse to recognize that we are greatly improving the present legislation by extending its implementation to services?
I believe it really should be said that Canada is almost the only country with a competition policy that does not apply to services. Among OECD countries, it seems that Ireland and Canada are the only countries that do not have any competition policy for services.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that this House will agree that it is more than time that our country lose this unenviable status. The great number of Canadian consumers who have complained to my department about restrictive practices in the field of services are wondering why this extension to the Act was not passed long ago.
Mr. Speaker, I notice that my time is getting short, and I would have liked to cover several issues raised by the hon. members but I will not have time to do so tonight. I would however like to say one thing, that not so long ago the Canadian public was brutally reminded that no legislation prevented the application in Canada of judgments, legislation or directives from foreign countries which are not in the interest of the Canadian public.
I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that this situation should be rectified urgently. This is precisely the purpose of Bill C-2, which will give the Commission the power to issue orders appropriate to each case of this type.
I believe that one of the issues raised concerns the recommendations of the Economic Council of Canada, and I would like to recall the remarks of the hon. member for York-Simcoe who stated in this House that there should be another report from the Economic Council of Canada. However, on page 2 of the third report of the Economic Council of Canada, it is said:
At first, we had considered a fourth report which would have summarized all the work done under these terms of reference, but we now believe that such a report would be redundant.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that this quotation from the third report is a sufficient reply to those who have blamed us for using a temporary report as a basis to review our competition policy.

October 28, 1974
Combines Investigation Act
Finally, I think that the point raised about the unions, to the effect that the government seems to be getting blamed for excluding them from this legislation, deserves clarification. In fact, the unions are excluded except for matters pertaining to collective bargaining. Such a situation was unacceptable. That is why, basically, all union activities recognized by this act were not subject to the first Canadian act of 1889 on competition, and this exclusion still stands.
Nowadays, both at the provincial and federal levels, there is a whole series of very specialized legislation on labour. There were reforms to be brought about and it is at the labour level that action must be taken. However, Bill C-2 clarifies several aspects of collective bargaining exclusions. I would like to point out, in particular, the clause of the bill specifying that the exclusions apply to management as well as to labour.	*
Mr. Speaker, I will conclude by saying that all the amendments in this bill concern the interests of the Canadian consumer maybe in a different way but always with equal importance. I am convinced that these interests are as badly served by restrictive schemes, resale price fixing and refusal to sell as they are by misleading advertising or pyramid selling. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I rather presented one bill only instead of including consumer protection legislation in a separate bill. I hope therefore that this bill will be examined with the warranted thoroughness by the members of the parliamentary committee and that we may report for third reading a bill really worthy of Canadians and of the competition policy in Canada.

subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR SERVICE BETWEEN EASTERN SASKATCHEWAN AND WESTERN MANITOBA-APPLICATION OF TRANSAIR FOR JET SERVICE
AIR TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR SERVICE BETWEEN EASTERN SASKATCHEWAN AND WESTERN MANITOBA-APPLICATION OF TRANSAIR FOR JET SERVICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 17 I raised a question with respect to air service into western Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan. I bring up the subject again tonight because of the confusion and mess in transportation policy that was referred to by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) in his celebrated statement last spring.
I will review the history of this service briefly. In the 1960s Air Canada inaugurated a service between Calgary and Saskatchewan and western Manitoba communities, on a daily basis, as part of a new regional air transport policy.
New runways were built at considerable cost in order to accommodate this service. Two years ago a brand new air terminal was opened at the Brandon airport to 'serve western Manitoba. It was considered an important breakthrough in air transport policy and the then Minister of Transport now the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), came out to open the terminal.
Last January all air service into the western Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan region was cancelled. That indeed indicates there is confusion if not a mess in air transport policy in this part of Canada. This development is in the face of expenditures of multimillions of dollars to build new airports to serve Montreal and Toronto.
Let me refer also to the STOL program costing either $125 million or $25 million depending on who is making the estimate to serve Ottawa and Montreal, the announcement that the government is to support a third-level carrier service, and also to the demonstrated fact that no program of regional economic development can make any progress unless adequate air service connects eastern Canada with western Canada.
During the election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) came to Winnipeg on May 23 and made some interesting comments. That is why I am making my appeal this evening. He said:
The general principles are that the policy of this government, as you know, is to work for all of Canada. We do this in different ways, but one of the most important ways of doing it is to make sure that every region of Canada shares in the growth of this country and that prosperity is accessible to all-
His statement continued to this effect:
... we have asked Air Canada to work with each provincial government to determine what action is necessary to put in place in each province a third-level air carrier system that will provide high quality local air service, promote industry, reduce isolation and provide jobs. Air Canada will then cooperate with the existing carriers in each province to put in place this service. Air Canada will, if necessary, either directly or through a subsidiary, provide that service. In other
October 28, 1974

instances, however, it will work with the existing carriers, supporting them financially by providing management back-up, by providing technical and maintenance know-how, and of course through the vast purchasing power of Air Canada.
Let me add that there is not much evidence of this in western Canada. Finally, may I quote from another part of the Prime Minister's statement. He said:
In another area of air service, air policy, industrial development and job creation, I would like to announce the following: approval in principle has been given by the government for the provision of air services linking Winnipeg, Brandon, Dauphin, Yorkton and Saskatoon as a test of possible new third-level air policies, the ones I talked about earlier. This will be air services linking these western cities.
I am sorry the Minister of Transport is not here. When he replied to my question originally he said that the government has purchased two Saunders aircraft which are to provide this service, but did not say who will operate the service. Will TransAir, the designated regional carrier, be responsible for providing this service? It will require a subsidy, as any other air service in Canada does, if we are to judge from the experience of Air Canada. If that is so, what will be the nature of the subsidy? Will it be similar to that provided for the demonstration STOL project now operating between Ottawa and Montreal? Finally, Madam Speaker, will it be supplemented by a first-class jet connection with eastern Canada?
TransAir, the designated regional carrier, now provides jet service to Dryden, Kenora, Thunder Bay and Toronto but, for inexplicable reasons, does not continue it to Brandon, Yorkton, Dauphin, Regina or Saskatoon. TransAir has had an application for almost six months before the Transport Committee, which seems to be in a state of suspended animation. The carrier has offered to provide this service without subsidy. It would provide direct, daily service to Toronto and the eastern market both ways; that is, by flying east and west, and would do this, as I say, without subsidy. In short, it would provide the kind of service which is absolutely essential for economic development programs on the Prairies. It would also supplement third-level carrier service. This would be a collector service which would make the pure jet service offered by TransAir economically viable. I trust that whoever replies this evening will answer these specific questions.

speakeroldname: Mr. Cliff Mclsaac (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AIR TRANSPORT-REQUEST FOR SERVICE BETWEEN EASTERN SASKATCHEWAN AND WESTERN MANITOBA-APPLICATION OF TRANSAIR FOR JET SERVICE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am afraid I cannot answer all the questions raised by the honourable member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale). I do not have the information available, but I assure him that I will check with regard to most, if not all, of the questions he raised. I am just as interested as the hon. member in the extension of air service to western Canada.
In his May 23 speech, to which the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) referred, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) stated that the federal government would make available $1.5 million for the purchase of two aircraft, plus spares, for a provincial demonstration project. The aircraft, of course, are to be ST-27 turbo prop manufactured, as the hon. member well knows, by the Saunders Aircraft Company in Gimli, Manitoba.
The federal government is awaiting a formal reply from the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan on whether they will embark on this demonstration project. I believe
Adjournment Debate
it is fair to say that negotiations are going well. Every indication is they will indeed go on with this, but as yet there has been no formal reply from them. Therefore the question as to when the demonstration services will start can be best answered by the provincial governments.
In the House the other day the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) announced that he had completed arrangements to purchase the two aircraft. The machinery has been set in motion for that.
The Prime Minister also stated that the Minister of Transport and Air Canada would put together a team of officials to work with the provinces. That is being done. A great deal of work has gone into it. Federal officials have assisted in every way with this demonstration project.
I can assure the hon. member I am also looking forward to the success of this particular service which is being inaugurated. Surveys have been conducted of the terminal and the other facilities. Information has been provided to the provinces to allow them to draw up a schedule for implementation of the demonstration project. The hon. member asked who will be operating the service. I do not know the answer to that.
With regard to the second part of the hon. member's question, the application by TransAir to bring jet service to Brandon and that region is, as the hon. member said, now before the air transport committee. I did not realize it had been there that long. The decision to grant a licence to TransAir rests entirely with the transport committee and not with the Department of Transport. We, of course, cannot interfere with the CTC while it is considering an application for a licence. I am hopeful that consideration will again be given to that request.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-MEASURES TO PROTECT PENSIONERS IN PRIVATE PLANS-DISCUSSIONS WITH CHARTERED BANKS
SOCIAL SECURITY-MEASURES TO PROTECT PENSIONERS IN PRIVATE PLANS-DISCUSSIONS WITH CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on Thursday, October 10, as recorded in Hansard at page 281, I put this question to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner):
Is the government giving consideration to the introduction this session of legislation regarding private pension plans, to provide greater protection for pensioners under those plans and to require such plans to comply with modern-day standards including the escalation of the pensions of those already retired?
In his answer the Minister of Finance suggested that my inquiry related to future legislation and that it had budgetary aspects which prevented him from replying fully to my question. I then posed a supplementary question in these terms:
In view of assurances the minister has given in former sessions, would he make a beginning on this subject by having further discussions with the chartered banks about their inadequate pension plans?
The minister's reply was to the effect that he had had discussions with the banks on previous occasions, but he thanked me for reminding him about the matter.
Your Honour, although I feel I should say Your Grace, my question is really a double barrelled one. In fact, there may be a third angle to it. However, it is an important issue, and I hope the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Cullen) is at least in a position to

October 28, 1974
Adjournment Debate
give me the assurance that the matters covered by my question are under active consideration.
I certainly do not want to exaggerate or to contribute to any sense of panic, but it is a fact that some pension plans have failed in recent months; it is a fact that there are a number of private pension plans which are in trouble, and the members of those plans are not sure they will get the pensions they were expecting. This is a situation which could get worse, and it seems to me that before it does it should be studied very thoroughly and the government should exercise its responsibility, bearing in mind the fact that the Department of Finance is in charge of legislation such as the Pension Benefits Standards Act. That is one aspect of the question-the need to protect the members of private pension plans, and I urge that this matter be given serious consideration.
Another aspect has to do with the question of the escalation of pensions. Thanks to efforts on the floor of this House this is now a fairly general practice in the public sector. But when private pension plans escalate pensions minus the escalation which takes place under our old age security legislation, those pensioners who are under private plans obtain no increase to enable them to keep up with the rising cost of living. Escalation is only effective if it applies to all of one's pension income. I hope the government will give consideration to legislation which will make this the rule for all pension plans.
These are the two important aspects of my question, but there was my subsidiary question about chartered banks and their pension plans. These come directly under the responsibility of the federal government in more ways than one. Some of the chartered banks are already offending their retired employees by subtracting from the escalation in their pensions the escalation which takes place under the Old Age Security Act. I could develop this point further if I had time in which to do so.
Many retired bank employees, some of whom were managers and who understandably do not not wish their names to be disclosed, are annoyed by the way the banks are treating them, and I hope the Minister of Finance will continue his conversations with the banks and talk to them in a way which will persuade them that they ought to play the game. The plain fact is that not only should all public pensions be escalated and made such that people can live on them, but this should also be true of all private pension plans, and I call on the government to see that this is done.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-MEASURES TO PROTECT PENSIONERS IN PRIVATE PLANS-DISCUSSIONS WITH CHARTERED BANKS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in response to the hon. member's question may I say I believe he will appreciate that there are a number of social, financial and jurisdictional considerations related to regulatory legislation of this kind.
It is necessary to bear in mind that the majority of the pension plans in Canada are subject to provincial jurisdiction. Up to the present four provinces have instituted pension benefits standards legislation. This legislation deals primarily with two aspects of pension plans, namely, plan solvency and benefit portability. The federal govern-

ment has already enacted similar legislation which applies to pension plans in areas of employment subject to the jurisdiction of parliament.
The only way in which the federal government could try to require and enforce the escalation of pension benefits in all plans would be indirectly through the Income Tax Act, where the normal penalty for non-compliance with such a requirement would be the probable deregistration of the plan, thereby making both employer and employee contributions to the plan ineligible for deduction from the income of the taxpayer. This could result in the employees being less well protected for their old age than they are at present.
It should be noted that neither of the forms of the legislation I have mentioned requires that an employer provide a pension plan. Nor does it prevent the termination of a plan. Some employers may be finding difficulty trying to fund their pension plans without provision for pension legislation. To impose compulsory escalation might well lead some employers to terminate the plans they have at present. In these circumstances hon. members will appreciate that requests such as those made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) must be considered with great caution.

TRANSPORT-REPORT ON PLANE CRASH NEAR FROBISHER BAY-REASON FOR DELAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I should like to congratulate the parliamentary secretary on his elevation to an important position in the ministry. My concern tonight arises from questions asked not only by myself but by others, Your Grace-and I refer to you in that manner because you do honour us-about a most unfortunate accident at Frobisher Bay last February. I welcome this opportunity because in response to questions the minister at one point said, and I refer to Hansard of October 4 at page 118:
No, Mr. Speaker, the truth cannot be changed, but sometimes it takes time to reveal the truth.
In the interest of accident investigation and transport safety generally in Canada, embracing all modes of transportation falling within the jurisdiction of the federal authority, I asked why there was not an investigation and report available from the coroner's inquest into that tragedy. Once again, I draw the attention of the minister to the urgency of separating the regulatory body from the responsibility of investigating all accidents involving any form of transportation falling within our jurisdiction.
I have a report in my hand of an aircraft accident to a Sabreliner CF-BRL on February 27, 1974, at Frobisher Bay, Northwest Territories. This report was made available to members on October 25, some eight months after the accident. I suggest that no competent investigative authority in North America or Europe would take more than three months to handle it. I cannot understand why this has taken so long.
Let me refer to one thing in this report to lend some emphasis to the point I make for the establishment of an independent commission of investigation in these matters. On the first page of the report under the paragraph head-
October 28, 1974

ing "Description of Occurrence" we find in the last paragraph:
The Frobisher main, high power non-direction beacon ... went off the air at 00:10 and was restored to service at 00:59.
All the times referred to are Greenwich mean time for the purpose of the investigation. Anyone reading this report will eventually reach page 7, and will find again in the last paragraph under the paragraph heading "Aids to Navigation" the following:
The operator coming on shift at 00:01 performed his routine station equipment check which included verifying the operation of the FY beacon. On the audio test the beacon went "in the red", a visual indication of a transmitter outage. The operator attempted to reset the transmitter-
The report indicates that the operator did those things that should be done under these circumstances.
I suggest that here we have a contradiction. This report will be read by everyone who flies the Atlantic in light aircraft or, indeed, in any type of aircraft. The purpose of these reports is to make corrections and see that mistakes do not recur to give concern to others using our system.
Here we have a discrepancy. There is nothing in the report to indicate how long the transmitter was inoperable prior to 00:01 hours on the date in question. It could very well have been out for a period even before that. My point is that if we are to foster and encourage confidence in our federal transport system on the part of those who use it, not only Canadians, but all users of our air space, then what we say must be accurate, must be complete and must be impartial.
I have no question about the impartiality of the investigator in this particular instance, but I suggest the publicity surrounding the coroner's inquest, and the division which will arise as a result of this report are such as to give rise to a belief that possibly a conflict of interest could take place in the investigation of transportation accidents in Canada.
I am here to bring to the attention of the parliamentary secretary as forcefully as possible my concern, and the concern of all users of our transportation services in Canada, that what we do not only must be right but that it must seem to be right. Where there is a conflict of interest we must remove it. In this case we cannot remove it until we remove some of the conflicts in respect of responsibility for investigations.
I would ask the parliamentary secretary to tell us why this report was not available to the coroner's inquest. I would also ask him when we might expect to have a bill introduced in respect of the division of the regulatory body. I have been asking for such a bill through four parliaments. If we had word from him about this I am sure the users of aids to navigation in air would have the type of confidence in our system which I know it merits.
Adjournment Debate

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-REPORT ON PLANE CRASH NEAR FROBISHER BAY-REASON FOR DELAY
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Halifax-Dartmouth East (Mr. Forrestall) has made, I believe, an excellent case for the division of the regulatory and investigative aspects of accidents of this kind. Perhaps I should review for him some of the pertinent dates in this regard relative to the report into the Sabreliner crash at Frobisher.
I am advised that the report was originally scheduled for completion sometime in mid-July, or a bit later. For reasons involving technical detail and checking into some of the material that was there, it was realized that it would take perhaps until mid-October before the results of the investigation could be completed. I am advised that on July 15 MOT officials met with the Crown Attorney and pointed out that it would be this late before the report would be available, and asked the coroner to delay the inquest until that time, or at least not look for the report until that time. However, as the hon. member is aware, the inquest was started on September 30 and the report was not available until October 9.
I think it is in respect of this aspect that some sort of an accusation was made, although it was not really an accusation, against the investigators. MOT officials were asked to comment on the report and they chose not to comment on it. They were very helpful in furnishing the facts at the coroner's inquest. I think this is what brought about the situation.
As the hon. member said, it was another situation in which some people might have felt there was a conflict of interest. I am satisfied there was not. The hon. member said he felt the same way. However, it points to the need to bring in legislation to separate the two functions because we have a good reputation, nationally and internationally, in investigations of this kind.
It has been the duty and the responsibility of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to carry out investigations, and I do not believe that there is any question that that has been done. But certainly if legislation can be introduced to make it even more true, that is what the government intends to do. I cannot tell the hon. member exactly when that legislation will be forthcoming, but I do believe it to be later on in this session, and I am sure the hon. member will have comments to make in the debate when it comes. I am sure he also appreciates some of the problems associated with the slight delay in tabling the report.
